lessons.title: Relationships and Foreign Keys
lessons.subtitle: Connect related tables and guarantee referential integrity using foreign keys and primary keys.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Model one-to-many relationships by connecting child rows to parent primary keys with REFERENCES foreign key constraints.

Real-World Scenario: An app tries to save an order for customer ID 500, but there is no customer with ID 500. What should happen? -> The foreign key should reject the order. This prevents an order from pointing to a customer who does not exist.

Big Picture: A relational database stores related information in separate tables and connects them with keys.

For example, one customer can place many orders. Each order belongs to one customer. The `orders.customer_id` column can point to `customers.id`.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. customers.id PRIMARY KEY: Uniquely identifies each customer record.
- 2. orders.customer_id: Stores the associated customer's ID for that specific order.
- 3. REFERENCES customers(id): Creates a foreign key constraint linking orders to customers.
- 4. Referential integrity enforcement: PostgreSQL rejects an order that refers to a customer ID that does not exist in the customers table.

Core Rule (Referential Integrity Rule): Every relationship column (like `customer_id` or `product_id`) must have a foreign key constraint pointing to the primary key of the parent table. Never rely solely on application code to enforce relationships.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Orphan Prevention: Foreign keys stop records from pointing to non-existent parent rows, guaranteeing referential consistency across all tables.
- One-to-Many Modeling: One customer can have many orders. Placing `customer_id` on the `orders` table models this classic 1:N cardinality cleanly.
- Index Foreign Keys: PostgreSQL does not automatically index foreign key columns. Always add an index to foreign key columns for fast joins and cascade deletes.

In Practice:
- Preventing Phantom Orders: If a frontend sends an order with an invalid or deleted customer ID, PostgreSQL rejects the `INSERT` immediately with a foreign key violation error.
- Cascade Options: PostgreSQL allows configuring `ON DELETE RESTRICT` (prevent deleting a customer who has orders) or `ON DELETE CASCADE` (automatically delete orders when customer is deleted).

Common Pitfall: Creating relational columns without a REFERENCES constraint, allowing ghost records that point to non-existent parents.

What to Avoid (Unconstrained Reference Column): Allows orphaned order records when customers are deleted or mistyped, breaking business reporting and invoicing.

Recommended Fix (Foreign Key with REFERENCES): The database rejects invalid customer IDs and enforces data integrity at all times.

Why It Matters: Referential integrity ensures that every transaction is connected to real entities, avoiding corrupted analytics and broken views.

Key Takeaways:
- Relational Links: Relational databases store related information in separate tables connected by keys.
- Foreign Key Invariants: A foreign key constraint ensures that a child row cannot reference a non-existent parent row.
- Prevent Orphan Rows: Foreign keys prevent orphaned records and protect data consistency across mutations.

lessons.title: JOIN — Read Data from Related Tables
lessons.subtitle: Combine data from multiple tables using INNER JOIN and preserve unmatched records with LEFT JOIN.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Combine related records across tables using INNER JOIN and preserve unmatched left-table records using inclusive LEFT JOINs.

Real-World Scenario: An admin wants to see all customers, including customers who have never placed an order. Which join should be used? -> Use LEFT JOIN with customers on the left. It keeps all customers and shows NULL for order information when no order exists.

Big Picture: A `JOIN` combines related rows from two or more tables. It is useful when the information you need is stored in different tables.

Suppose customer names are in `customers` and order totals are in `orders`.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Table scanning: PostgreSQL reads rows from both `customers` and `orders`.
- 2. Join predicate (ON): `ON orders.customer_id = customers.id` specifies the matching condition linking the tables.
- 3. INNER JOIN semantics: Returns only pairs of rows where a matching customer and matching order both exist.
- 4. LEFT JOIN semantics: Preserves every row from the left table (`customers`), filling in `NULL` for order columns when no matching order exists.

Core Rule (Join Selection Rule): Use `INNER JOIN` when you only care about records that possess related data on both sides. Use `LEFT JOIN` when you need to preserve all records from the primary table regardless of whether children exist.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Exact Intersections: INNER JOIN drops customers who haven't ordered yet and drops any orphaned orders. It only returns verified relationships.
- Inclusive LEFT JOIN: LEFT JOIN guarantees that every left row appears in the output, allowing reports to show inactive customers or unassigned tickets.
- Explicit ON Conditions: Always specify exact join predicates with `ON`. Forgetting `ON` causes a Cartesian product (CROSS JOIN) multiplying all rows.

In Practice:
- Sales Report (INNER JOIN): When calculating total store revenue for customers who actually bought items, `INNER JOIN` ensures only real sales are included.
- Customer Engagement Audit (LEFT JOIN): To find registered customers who have never made a purchase, use `LEFT JOIN` and filter for `WHERE orders.id IS NULL`.

Common Pitfall: Using an INNER JOIN when generating a full customer list, accidentally filtering out all newly registered customers who haven't purchased yet.

What to Avoid (Inadvertently Omitting Inactive Users): Customers who signed up recently or have zero purchases disappear completely from customer management lists.

Recommended Fix (Inclusive LEFT JOIN with Fallback): Shows every customer in the database, displaying 0.00 or NULL if they have not placed an order.

Why It Matters: Choosing the wrong join type can silently exclude customers, leading to skewed analytics and broken customer support dashboards.

Key Takeaways:
- JOIN Combines Relations: Joins connect normalized tables based on shared key relationships defined in `ON` clauses.
- INNER vs LEFT: `INNER JOIN` requires matches on both sides; `LEFT JOIN` preserves all rows from the left table.
- Spotting Inactive Records: Use `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right_table.id IS NULL` to identify unassociated or inactive records.

codeBlocks.title: JOIN — Read Data from Related Tables
codeBlocks.code:
-- INNER JOIN: returns rows where a match exists in both tables
SELECT customers.name, orders.total
FROM customers
INNER JOIN orders
  ON orders.customer_id = customers.id;

-- LEFT JOIN: keeps every customer even if they have no orders
SELECT customers.name, orders.total
FROM customers
LEFT JOIN orders
  ON orders.customer_id = customers.id;

codeBlocks.title: Inadvertently Omitting Inactive Users
codeBlocks.code:
-- Flawed: Drops all customers with 0 orders!
SELECT customers.name, orders.total
FROM customers
INNER JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id;

codeBlocks.title: Inclusive LEFT JOIN with Fallback
codeBlocks.code:
-- Production: Keeps all customers
SELECT customers.name, COALESCE(orders.total, 0.00) AS order_total
FROM customers
LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id;

lessons.title: Aggregate Functions, GROUP BY, and HAVING
lessons.subtitle: Calculate summary metrics with COUNT, SUM, and AVG, group rows by category, and filter aggregate results with HAVING.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Calculate summary metrics with COUNT, SUM, and AVG, segment records with GROUP BY, and filter grouped calculations with HAVING.

Real-World Scenario: You need to show only products with more than 100 sales. Where should you filter the calculated sale count? -> Use HAVING after GROUP BY, because the condition applies to the calculated count for each product group.

Big Picture: Aggregate functions calculate one result from many rows. Common examples are `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, and `MAX`.

Use `GROUP BY` to calculate a result for each group. Use `HAVING` to filter the groups after the calculation.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. FROM orders: PostgreSQL reads all candidate rows from the orders table.
- 2. GROUP BY customer_id: Buckets rows into distinct groups based on matching `customer_id` values.
- 3. COUNT(*): Calculates the total number of orders in each customer group.
- 4. SUM(total): Sums the `total` column across all rows in each group.
- 5. HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2: Filters the calculated groups, keeping only customers who have placed at least two orders.

Core Rule (WHERE vs HAVING Rule): Use `WHERE` to filter individual rows *before* grouping occurs. Use `HAVING` to filter the aggregated group results *after* calculation. Never put aggregate functions inside a `WHERE` clause.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Mathematical Summaries: `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, and `MAX` compress multiple rows into a single scalar value per group.
- Grouping Keys: Every column in your SELECT list must either appear in the `GROUP BY` clause or be wrapped in an aggregate function.
- Post-Aggregation Filtering: Because aggregate results do not exist until rows are grouped, filtering by those calculations requires `HAVING`.

In Practice:
- VIP Customer Loyalty Analysis: To reward repeat buyers, query the orders table grouped by customer ID with `HAVING SUM(total) > 5000` to find high-value VIP accounts.
- Combining WHERE and HAVING: `WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01'` filters out old orders first, then `GROUP BY customer_id HAVING count(*) >= 3` finds frequent buyers this year.

Common Pitfall: Attempting to filter an aggregate calculation inside a WHERE clause, which triggers a syntax error in SQL.

What to Avoid (Aggregate in WHERE Clause): SQL processes WHERE before calculating aggregates. The count does not exist yet when WHERE runs.

Recommended Fix (Correct HAVING Clause): Correctly filters the aggregated result set after group calculations are complete.

Why It Matters: Understanding query execution order (FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY) prevents common SQL runtime errors.

Key Takeaways:
- Summarizing Many Rows: Aggregate functions (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`) compute single metrics from sets of rows.
- GROUP BY Creates Buckets: Use `GROUP BY` to segment calculations across categories, users, or dates.
- WHERE vs HAVING: `WHERE` filters input rows before grouping; `HAVING` filters calculated metrics after grouping.

codeBlocks.title: Aggregate Functions, GROUP BY, and HAVING
codeBlocks.code:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count,
       SUM(total) AS amount_spent
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;

codeBlocks.title: Aggregate in WHERE Clause
codeBlocks.code:
-- Syntax Error in PostgreSQL: aggregate functions not allowed in WHERE
SELECT customer_id, count(*)
FROM orders
WHERE count(*) >= 2 -- Invalid!
GROUP BY customer_id;

codeBlocks.title: Correct HAVING Clause
codeBlocks.code:
-- Production: Valid SQL grouping and post-filter
SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING count(*) >= 2;

codeBlocks.title: Interactive SQL Sandbox
codeBlocks.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  total NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, total) VALUES
  (1, 250.00),
  (1, 400.00),
  (1, 150.00),
  (2, 80.00),
  (3, 900.00),
  (3, 1200.00);

SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count, SUM(total) AS amount_spent
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;

lessons.title: Subqueries and Common Table Expressions (CTEs)
lessons.subtitle: Break complex SQL transformations into readable steps using nested subqueries and named CTEs with the WITH clause.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Break complex analytical transformations into clean, readable, modular steps using nested subqueries and named CTEs with the WITH clause.

Real-World Scenario: A report query is becoming difficult to read because it contains a calculation inside another query. What could make it clearer? -> A CTE can give the calculation a name and separate it from the main query. It can make the SQL easier to read, although it is not automatically faster than a subquery.

Big Picture: A **subquery** is a query used inside another query. A **CTE** is a named result created with `WITH`, which can make a longer query easier to read.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Inner subquery: The nested subquery `(SELECT AVG(price) FROM products)` computes the single average price value first.
- 2. Outer query comparison: The outer query filters rows whose individual price exceeds that computed scalar average.
- 3. WITH customer_totals AS (...) : Creates a named Common Table Expression (CTE) holding the aggregated customer spendings.
- 4. Main query execution: The outer query cleanly selects from `customer_totals` and applies business filters (`WHERE spent > 5000`).

Core Rule (Query Modularity Rule): Use CTEs (`WITH`) to name intermediate datasets and simplify multi-step analytics. While modern PostgreSQL optimizes CTEs inline with subqueries, CTEs provide far superior readability and team maintainability.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Linear Top-to-Bottom Flow: CTEs read like variable declarations in standard programming languages, making complex business logic easy to audit.
- Scalar Lookups: Use quick inline subqueries for dynamic scalar thresholds like `WHERE created_at > (SELECT max(...) FROM ...)`.
- Chained CTEs: You can chain multiple CTEs with commas (`WITH a AS (...), b AS (...) SELECT ...`) to construct elegant analytical pipelines.

In Practice:
- Multi-Tier Customer Segmentation: Compute order totals in CTE 1, classify customers into Gold/Silver tiers in CTE 2, and aggregate tier performance in the final query.
- Subquery in WHERE IN: `WHERE id IN (SELECT product_id FROM active_promotions)` lets you filter against dynamic lists from other tables cleanly.

Common Pitfall: Writing deeply nested subqueries 4 levels deep in FROM and WHERE clauses, making queries unreadable and hard to debug.

What to Avoid (Hard-to-Read Deeply Nested Subquery): Extremely difficult to read, debug, and maintain as business requirements evolve.

Recommended Fix (Clean Modular Common Table Expression (CTE)): Each step is isolated, named clearly, and easily verified independently.

Why It Matters: Readable SQL reduces maintenance bugs, speeds up code reviews, and simplifies performance troubleshooting.

Key Takeaways:
- Subquery Inside Query: A subquery is a nested SQL statement executed within an outer query.
- CTEs for Clean Organization: Use `WITH` to name intermediate calculations and make multi-step SQL readable.
- Maintainability Win: CTEs make complex analytical queries easier to read and test than deeply nested subqueries.

codeBlocks.title: Subqueries and Common Table Expressions (CTEs)
codeBlocks.code:
-- Subquery example: find products priced above average
SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE price > (
  SELECT AVG(price)
  FROM products
);

-- CTE example: named intermediate result with WITH
WITH customer_totals AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spent
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT customer_id, spent
FROM customer_totals
WHERE spent > 5000;

codeBlocks.title: Hard-to-Read Deeply Nested Subquery
Clean Modular Common Table Expression (CTE)
codeBlocks.code:
WITH active_customers AS (
  SELECT id FROM customers WHERE is_active = TRUE
),
customer_spending AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spent
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT customer_id, spent
FROM customer_spending
WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM active_customers)
  AND spent > 1000;

codeBlocks.code:
CREATE TABLE products (
  id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  price NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO products (name, price) VALUES
  ('Mechanical Keyboard', 1200.00),
  ('Mouse Pad', 200.00),
  ('4K Monitor', 4500.00),
  ('HDMI Cable', 150.00);

-- Query products priced above the overall catalog average:
WITH catalog_stats AS (
  SELECT AVG(price) AS avg_price
  FROM products
)
SELECT p.name, p.price, round(s.avg_price, 2) AS catalog_avg
FROM products p, catalog_stats s
WHERE p.price > s.avg_price;

lessons.title: UPDATE Carefully and Use RETURNING
lessons.subtitle: Execute safe modifications and retrieve mutated, generated, or deleted rows in a single round-trip with RETURNING.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Execute targeted updates and eliminate extra SELECT roundtrips by returning mutated or inserted rows directly using PostgreSQL's RETURNING clause.

Real-World Scenario: An application changes a customer's email and needs the updated row immediately. What can it use? -> It can use UPDATE ... RETURNING to change the email and get the updated row in the same statement.

Big Picture: `UPDATE` changes existing rows. PostgreSQL's `RETURNING` clause can show the rows that were changed.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. UPDATE products: Selects the target table to modify.
- 2. SET price = 1400: Assigns the new price value to matching rows.
- 3. WHERE id = 10: Restricts the mutation to the single product with ID 10.
- 4. RETURNING id, name, price: Returns the modified row immediately to the client without requiring a second SELECT query.

Core Rule (Atomic Mutation Return Rule): Use `RETURNING` with `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` to fetch generated IDs, updated timestamps, or deleted snapshots atomically in a single network round-trip.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Fetch Generated IDs: `INSERT INTO customers (...) RETURNING id;` immediately provides the generated primary key to your backend code.
- Verify Mutations: RETURNING confirms the exact updated state and verifies whether any rows actually matched the WHERE condition.
- Archive Snapshots: `DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expired_at < NOW() RETURNING *;` lets you log or archive purged records seamlessly.

In Practice:
- User Profile Updates: When a user edits their profile, `UPDATE users SET name = $1, email = $2 WHERE id = $3 RETURNING *` immediately sends the fresh user object back to the client application.
- Checking for 0 Rows Affected: If the RETURNING clause returns an empty array, your application knows immediately that no row matched the ID (e.g. 404 Not Found) without a separate lookup.

Common Pitfall: Executing an UPDATE followed by an immediate SELECT, introducing network latency and concurrency race conditions.

What to Avoid (Two-Query Write and Read): Doubles database network latency. Another concurrent transaction could modify the row between the UPDATE and SELECT.

Recommended Fix (Single Roundtrip with RETURNING): Halves latency and returns the exact snapshot produced by that specific UPDATE statement.

Why It Matters: RETURNING provides atomic, race-free verification of mutations while saving database bandwidth and reducing connection overhead.

Key Takeaways:
- Immediate Feedback: `RETURNING` shows the exact rows modified, created, or removed by a mutation.
- Saves Network Roundtrips: Eliminates the need for a secondary `SELECT` after `INSERT` or `UPDATE`.
- Works with All Mutations: Use `RETURNING` across `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` commands.

codeBlocks.title: UPDATE Carefully and Use RETURNING
codeBlocks.code:
UPDATE products
SET price = 1400
WHERE id = 10
RETURNING id, name, price;

codeBlocks.title: Two-Query Write and Read
Single Roundtrip with RETURNING
codeBlocks.code:
-- Production: Atomic single roundtrip
UPDATE products
SET price = 1400
WHERE id = 10
RETURNING id, name, price;

codeBlocks.title: Interactive SQL Sandbox
codeBlocks.code:
CREATE TABLE products (
  id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  price NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL
);

-- Insert and return generated ID:
INSERT INTO products (name, price)
VALUES ('Smart Watch', 499.00)
RETURNING id, name, price;

-- Update and return modified row:
UPDATE products
SET price = 449.00
WHERE name = 'Smart Watch'
RETURNING id, name, price;

lessons.title: Transactions and ACID
lessons.subtitle: Group related SQL operations into atomic units with BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK, and master the four ACID guarantees.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Guarantee all-or-nothing execution with BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK, and master the four ACID guarantees that protect financial data.

Real-World Scenario: A money transfer subtracts money from the first account, but adding it to the second account fails. What should the application do? -> It should roll back the transaction so the first subtraction is not saved by itself. Both parts of the transfer must succeed together.

Big Picture: A transaction groups multiple database actions into one unit. The goal is to make sure the related actions succeed together or are undone together.

Imagine transferring 500 from one bank account to another. The system must subtract 500 from one account and add 500 to the other. It must not finish only half of the transfer.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. BEGIN: Opens a new transactional unit of work.
- 2. First UPDATE (Debit): Subtracts 500 from account 1.
- 3. Second UPDATE (Credit): Adds 500 to account 2.
- 4. COMMIT: Persists both changes permanently and atomically to disk.
- 5. ROLLBACK safety: If any step encounters an error or crash before commit, `ROLLBACK` undoes all interim changes as if they never happened.

Core Rule (ACID Transaction Guarantees Rule): Whenever two or more mutations must succeed or fail as a single logical unit of work, enclose them in `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`. Always issue `ROLLBACK` in catch/error handlers.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- All or Nothing: All modifications inside the transaction boundary commit successfully, or all changes are completely rolled back.
- Constraint Invariants: A transaction cannot leave the database in an invalid state; all table constraints and rules must be satisfied upon commit.
- Concurrency & Durability: Isolation prevents concurrent transactions from seeing uncommitted intermediate states. Durability guarantees committed writes survive power loss.

In Practice:
- Order Placement and Inventory Deduction: Creating an order record and decrementing inventory must happen together. If inventory is out of stock, rolling back the transaction ensures no orphan order record is created.
- Connection Loss Recovery: If the database connection drops while executing statements before `COMMIT`, PostgreSQL automatically aborts and rolls back the uncommitted transaction.

Common Pitfall: Running multi-step mutations without a transaction block, leaving partial writes in the database on error.

What to Avoid (Unprotected Multi-Step Mutations): Leaves the database in an inconsistent state where money has vanished from account 1.

Recommended Fix (Protected Transaction Block): Guarantees that money is only deducted if it is successfully credited to the destination account.

Why It Matters: Transactions prevent incomplete business operations and are the bedrock of reliable financial and order processing systems.

Key Takeaways:
- Keep Changes Together: Transactions ensure that multi-step mutations either complete as a whole or leave no partial changes.
- BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK: Start with `BEGIN`, save with `COMMIT`, and cancel with `ROLLBACK` on error.
- The Four ACID Pillars: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid rules), Isolation (independent concurrency), Durability (permanent storage).

lessons.title: Database Design and Normalization
lessons.subtitle: Organize schemas to eliminate redundancy, avoid update anomalies, and connect entities with foreign keys.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Design clean relational schemas to eliminate redundancy, avoid update anomalies, and maintain a strict single source of truth.

Real-World Scenario: A customer's email is copied into 20 order rows. The customer changes their email. What design problem does this create? -> The same information is repeated in many places. Some rows could be missed during an update. Store the email once in the customers table and connect orders using a foreign key.

Big Picture: Database design is deciding how information should be split into tables and how those tables should be connected.

**Problem: repeating customer details in every order:**

A badly designed table might store customer name and email on every order row. If the customer changes their email, many rows may need updating. Some rows could be missed.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Dedicated customers table: Stores customer details in one authoritative location.
- 2. Dedicated orders table: Stores order-specific data such as total and timestamp.
- 3. Foreign key reference: Each order stores the customer's ID instead of duplicating customer name and email across every row.
- 4. Single source of truth: Updating a customer's email requires changing only one row in `customers`, automatically updating the customer's profile across all past and future orders.
- 5. On-demand joining: The application uses an efficient SQL `JOIN` whenever it needs both customer and order attributes together.

Core Rule (Single Source of Truth Rule): Every distinct fact should exist in exactly one place in your database. Separate distinct real-world entities into separate tables and connect them using foreign keys.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Eliminating Update Anomalies: If an address is duplicated across 50 orders, updating it in 49 rows leaves the 50th in a desynchronized state. Normalization stores it once.
- Practical Normalization: You don't need to memorize academic normal forms on day one; focus on identifying distinct entities and avoiding repeated string blocks.
- Storage & Cache Efficiency: Storing integer foreign keys (8 bytes) instead of repeated customer names and emails (50+ bytes per row) saves massive amounts of disk and RAM.

In Practice:
- Product Catalog Updates: When a merchant renames a product, storing `product_id` in order items means the product name only changes in one row in the `products` table.
- Historical Snapshot Nuance: For prices charged at the moment of checkout, order items store a copy of the historical price paid (`unit_price`), because catalog prices fluctuate over time.

Common Pitfall: Creating a single flat table that denormalizes customer names, emails, and phone numbers into every order row.

What to Avoid (Duplicated Denormalized Table): If the customer updates their email, old orders display stale data or require updating thousands of rows.

Recommended Fix (Normalized Relational Architecture): Customer data is updated in one row; orders link to it via customer_id.

Why It Matters: Proper database design prevents data inconsistency, simplifies schema migrations, and saves database storage.

Key Takeaways:
- Separate Entities: Store distinct entities (customers, products, orders) in dedicated tables.
- Connect with Foreign Keys: Use foreign keys to link tables rather than copying repetitive text.
- Prevent Update Anomalies: Single-source-of-truth tables ensure that updates happen in one place.

codeBlocks.title: Database Design and Normalization
Duplicated Denormalized Table
codeBlocks.code:
-- Flawed: repeating customer details across every order
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id INT,
  customer_name TEXT,
  customer_email TEXT, -- Copied into every single order!
  order_total NUMERIC
);

lessons.title: Indexes — Find Rows Faster
lessons.subtitle: Accelerate query performance with B-Tree indexes while understanding write overhead and storage trade-offs.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Accelerate query lookups with B-Tree indexes, identify when to index foreign keys, and balance read speed against insert/update overhead.

Real-World Scenario: An orders table has millions of rows, and searching by customer_id is slow. What can you investigate? -> Check the query plan and consider an index on customer_id. Then measure the query again to see whether it improved.

Big Picture: An index is a data structure PostgreSQL can use to find rows without checking every row in the table. It can make some searches faster, but it also uses storage and adds work when data changes.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id: Creates a B-Tree index on the `customer_id` column of the `orders` table.
- 2. Maintenance on mutations: PostgreSQL automatically updates the B-Tree index whenever rows are inserted, updated, or deleted.
- 3. Fast index lookup: When a query filters by `customer_id = 25`, PostgreSQL can navigate the B-Tree in O(log N) operations to locate target rows directly.
- 4. Planner cost decision: The query planner decides whether using the index is cheaper than a sequential scan based on table statistics and row selectivity.

Core Rule (Index Trade-Off Rule): Index frequently filtered columns, foreign keys, and unique constraints. Do not index every column indiscriminately, as every index increases write latency and disk consumption.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- O(log N) Lookups: Indexes allow jumping directly to matching rows without scanning the full table, reducing query response times from seconds to microseconds.
- Insert / Update Costs: Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` must update every index on the table, adding CPU and write I/O overhead.
- Disk & Memory Footprint: Indexes consume RAM in the PostgreSQL buffer pool. Over-indexing starves data caches and harms overall database throughput.

In Practice:
- Indexing Foreign Keys: PostgreSQL creates indexes for PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraints automatically, but does NOT create an index on `FOREIGN KEY` columns. Always index foreign keys like `orders.customer_id`.
- Small Table Exception: On tables with only a few hundred rows (like a `roles` or `order_status` table), a sequential scan is often faster than an index scan because the entire table fits in a single memory block.

Common Pitfall: Failing to index foreign keys or frequently queried search columns in tables with millions of rows.

What to Avoid (Missing Index on Foreign Key): Causes massive disk I/O and CPU spikes, slowing down customer order history pages.

Recommended Fix (Targeted B-Tree Index): Reduces execution time by over 99% while conserving server CPU and memory.

Why It Matters: Strategic indexing is the single most effective way to optimize relational query response times under high scale.

Key Takeaways:
- Speed Up Searches: Indexes allow PostgreSQL to locate matching rows without scanning every row in the table.
- Write Trade-Off: Indexes accelerate reads but add computational overhead and storage costs to writes.
- Index Foreign Keys: Always index foreign key columns to ensure joins and parent updates run fast.

codeBlocks.title: Indexes — Find Rows Faster
Missing Index on Foreign Key
codeBlocks.code:
-- Flawed: 10 million row orders table with NO index on customer_id
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;

-- Results in: Sequential Scan on orders (cost=0.00..184562.00 rows=3 width=48)
-- Reads all 10,000,000 rows from disk every query!

lessons.title: Read a Query Plan with EXPLAIN
lessons.subtitle: Diagnose query bottlenecks, inspect Seq Scan vs Index Scan, and measure actual execution with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS).
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Dissect optimizer query execution plans, identify sequential table scans vs index scans, and measure actual execution with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS).

Real-World Scenario: A developer adds an index but the query is still slow. What should they check next? -> Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and look at the actual plan, rows, and time. PostgreSQL may have chosen not to use the index, or another part of the query may be the real problem.

Big Picture: `EXPLAIN` shows how PostgreSQL plans to run a query. It helps you understand whether PostgreSQL expects to scan a table, use an index, join tables, or perform other work.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. EXPLAIN estimation: Shows the query execution plan without running the statement, displaying estimated startup cost and total cost.
- 2. Scan node types: Reveals whether PostgreSQL chooses a `Seq Scan` (reading the entire table) or an `Index Scan` / `Bitmap Index Scan`.
- 3. ANALYZE option: Actually executes the query to measure actual runtime in milliseconds (`actual time=0.042..0.085`) and rows returned.
- 4. BUFFERS option: Reports memory buffer hits (`shared hit=3`) vs physical disk reads (`read=12`).
- 5. Safety note: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually executes the query! Running it with an `UPDATE` or `DELETE` will modify database data.

Core Rule (Query Plan Diagnostics Rule): Diagnose slow queries using `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`. Look for unexpected `Seq Scan` nodes on large tables and check for discrepancies between estimated and actual row counts.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Seq Scan vs Index Scan: Seq Scan reads all table blocks sequentially. Index Scan uses B-Tree pointers to read only relevant rows.
- Shared Buffer Hits: Buffer hits indicate data was served from RAM. High buffer reads from disk identify I/O bottlenecks.
- ANALYZE Executes: Remember that ANALYZE executes the statement. Always wrap tests in a rolled-back transaction if testing mutations (`BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE ...; ROLLBACK;`).

In Practice:
- Stale Statistics: If the planner expects 5 rows (`rows=5`) but the query returns 500,000 rows (`actual rows=500000`), run `ANALYZE table_name;` to update PostgreSQL's planner statistics.
- Index Ignored Due to Type Mismatch: If a column is `BIGINT` and your query passes a string or calls a function on the column (`WHERE lower(email) = ...`), PostgreSQL cannot use standard indexes.

Common Pitfall: Guessing which indexes to add without inspecting the EXPLAIN plan, or running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a DELETE statement in production.

What to Avoid (Blind Optimization): Adds write overhead without solving the actual query bottleneck.

Recommended Fix (Plan-Driven Optimization): Identifies the exact step consuming execution time with empirical measurements.

Why It Matters: Data-driven query tuning solves real production bottlenecks without adding useless indexes.

Key Takeaways:
- Understand Planner Choices: `EXPLAIN` displays whether PostgreSQL plans to scan a table, use an index, or join data.
- Measure Real Runtimes: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` executes the query to report actual times and buffer hits.
- Verify Before and After: Always compare query plans before and after adding an index to verify performance improvements.

codeBlocks.title: Read a Query Plan with EXPLAIN
codeBlocks.code:
-- Shows planned steps based on optimizer cost estimates
EXPLAIN
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 25;

-- Actually runs the query and displays real timings and buffer usage
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 25;

lessons.title: Views
lessons.subtitle: Encapsulate reusable, complex queries as virtual tables that simplify reports and secure sensitive columns.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Encapsulate reusable, complex queries into virtual tables that simplify application code, centralize business logic, and protect sensitive columns.

Real-World Scenario: Several reports need the same customer order summary. How can a view help? -> Create a view containing the shared summary query. Each report can read from the view instead of repeating the same SQL.

Big Picture: A view is a saved SQL query that you can read like a table. A normal view stores the query, not a separate copy of its result.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. CREATE VIEW order_summaries: Saves the query specification into the database catalog under a virtual table name.
- 2. Aggregation query definition: The underlying query aggregates orders by customer and computes order counts and spending totals.
- 3. Clean client consumption: Applications and BI reports query `order_summaries` directly using standard SELECT, WHERE, and ORDER BY syntax.
- 4. Dynamic evaluation: A standard view executes against underlying tables on demand; it does not store a stale duplicate copy of the data on disk.

Core Rule (View Encapsulation Rule): Use standard views to simplify complex joins and aggregations into clean virtual tables. Understand that standard views compute results dynamically on each query without consuming separate table storage.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- DRY Query Logic: Define intricate 4-table joins once in a view. All microservices and reporting dashboards query the view consistently.
- Column Security Masking: Create views that omit sensitive columns (e.g. `user_public_profiles` excludes `password_hash` and `ssn`) and grant permissions only to the view.
- Zero Duplicate Storage: Standard views do not duplicate row data on disk. When data in the underlying table changes, the view immediately reflects the update.

In Practice:
- Shared Business Definitions: If the definition of an 'active paying customer' involves filtering orders and excluding refunds, putting that logic in a view ensures marketing and finance report matching numbers.
- Materialized Views (Future Study): For massive multi-million-row aggregations that run infrequently, PostgreSQL also offers `MATERIALIZED VIEW` which caches the computed result on disk and can be refreshed periodically.

Common Pitfall: Copying and pasting a 50-line analytical join query into 12 different API routes and reporting scripts.

What to Avoid (Duplicated Analytical SQL): When business logic changes (e.g. excluding cancelled orders), developers must update all 12 routes; missing one causes data discrepancies.

Recommended Fix (Encapsulated Database View): Centralizes logic in one place. Updating the view updates all consumers instantly.

Why It Matters: Views provide maintainable abstraction boundaries, keeping application code clean and business logic centralized.

Key Takeaways:
- Virtual Tables: A view is a saved SQL query that can be queried just like a regular table.
- Dynamic Evaluation: Standard views read live data from base tables without duplicating data on disk.
- Centralized Logic: Views centralize complex joins and calculations so all application consumers share consistent definitions.

codeBlocks.title: Views
codeBlocks.code:
CREATE VIEW order_summaries AS
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count,
       SUM(total) AS total_spent
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;

-- Read directly from the view:
SELECT *
FROM order_summaries
WHERE total_spent > 5000;

codeBlocks.title: Duplicated Analytical SQL
Encapsulated Database View
codeBlocks.code:
CREATE VIEW customer_sales_overview AS
SELECT c.id, c.name, count(o.id) AS order_count, sum(o.total) AS total_revenue
FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status != 'cancelled'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

-- All API routes now query:
SELECT * FROM customer_sales_overview WHERE total_revenue > 1000;

lessons.title: JSONB — Store and Read JSON Data
lessons.subtitle: Store flexible, semi-structured document payloads alongside relational columns and query attributes using the ->> operator.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Leverage hybrid relational-document storage in PostgreSQL by storing semi-structured JSON payloads and extracting fields with the ->> operator.

Real-World Scenario: Products have optional details that differ by category, such as screen size for laptops and material for chairs. How could JSONB help? -> A JSONB column can store category-specific details that do not fit the same fixed set of columns. Keep common fields like name and price as normal columns.

Big Picture: PostgreSQL is a relational database, but it can also store JSON data. `JSONB` stores JSON in a form that PostgreSQL can query and index.

Use normal columns for important, predictable fields. Use `JSONB` when some data has a flexible shape and you still need to store it in PostgreSQL.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. details JSONB: Defines a column using PostgreSQL's binary JSON format, which parses and validates JSON on insert.
- 2. Casting with ::jsonb: Casts raw JSON strings into binary JSONB objects.
- 3. The ->> operator: Extracts a JSON object property as standard SQL `TEXT` (while `->` extracts the property as a nested JSON object).
- 4. Hybrid relational modeling: Returns relational columns (`name`) and document attributes (`color`) together seamlessly in standard SQL result rows.

Core Rule (Hybrid Relational-Document Rule): Keep predictable, relational attributes (IDs, foreign keys, prices, statuses) as strongly-typed relational columns. Use `JSONB` only for polymorphic or dynamic attributes that vary widely across records.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- JSON vs JSONB: Always use `JSONB` instead of plain `JSON`. `JSONB` stores decomposed binary data, eliminating re-parsing on every query and supporting GIN indexing.
- Arrow Operators (-> vs ->>): `->` extracts a JSON element (useful for chaining nested objects), while `->>` extracts the value as plain text for filtering and display.
- GIN Index Support: PostgreSQL allows creating GIN indexes on JSONB columns (`CREATE INDEX ON products USING GIN (details);`) for ultra-fast document search.

In Practice:
- E-Commerce Category Attributes: Laptops have `ram` and `screen_size`; shoes have `shoe_size` and `color`; books have `isbn` and `page_count`. Storing these in a `metadata JSONB` column avoids schema bloat.
- Filtering by JSON Properties: `WHERE details ->> 'color' = 'black'` lets you filter products by nested document attributes using standard SQL clauses.

Common Pitfall: Dumping the entire application schema into a single JSONB column, losing all relational types, constraints, and foreign key guarantees.

What to Avoid (Anti-Pattern: Complete Denormalization into JSONB): Loses NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE, and FOREIGN KEY protection; arithmetic becomes slow and error-prone.

Recommended Fix (Production Hybrid Model): Enforces strict financial and relational invariants while offering flexible document storage for variable fields.

Why It Matters: Balancing relational rigor with JSONB flexibility gives you the best of both worlds without sacrificing data integrity.

Key Takeaways:
- Relational + Document: PostgreSQL combines relational tables with powerful semi-structured `JSONB` storage.
- Use ->> for Text: Use `->>` to extract nested values as text for display or filtering.
- Keep Core Fields Relational: Always keep IDs, foreign keys, and prices as strongly typed relational columns.

lessons.title: Pagination — Return Data in Small Pages
lessons.subtitle: Implement performant data pagination using standard LIMIT/OFFSET and scalable Keyset cursor pagination.
lessons.stageName: Work with Data Efficiently and Safely
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Avoid transferring massive datasets using LIMIT/OFFSET pagination, and master high-performance Keyset cursor pagination for large tables.

Real-World Scenario: A product table has 500,000 rows. Should the API return all rows for one page? -> No. It should return a small page of rows. This reduces the amount of data sent and processed at one time.

Big Picture: Pagination splits a large result into smaller pages. It avoids sending every row to the application at once.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. ORDER BY id: Establishes a stable, deterministic sort order essential for reliable page boundaries.
- 2. OFFSET 20: Instructs PostgreSQL to discard the first 20 rows of the ordered result set.
- 3. LIMIT 10: Returns the next 10 rows (representing Page 3 of 10 items per page).
- 4. Keyset cursor approach: Instead of scanning and discarding skipped rows, keyset pagination uses `WHERE id > last_seen_id LIMIT 10` to jump straight to the next page using an index.

Core Rule (Deterministic Pagination Rule): Always paginate high-cardinality tables. For small tables or jump-to-page UIs, `LIMIT/OFFSET` is acceptable. For large tables or infinite feeds, use keyset cursor pagination (`WHERE id > :cursor`). Always enforce a deterministic `ORDER BY`.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Offset Degradation: `OFFSET 100000` forces the engine to read and discard 100,000 rows before returning row 100,001, causing latency spikes on deep pages.
- Keyset Cursor Efficiency: Keyset pagination relies on B-Tree index navigation (`WHERE id > 20`), ensuring Page 10,000 runs as fast as Page 1.
- Preventing Missing/Duplicate Items: If new rows are inserted while a user browses, OFFSET causes rows to shift and duplicate. Keyset cursors remain rock-solid.

In Practice:
- E-Commerce Category Listings: Showing 24 products per page with pagination links (1, 2, 3...) typically uses `LIMIT 24 OFFSET (page - 1) * 24`.
- Mobile App Infinite Scrolling: Infinite feeds request `GET /api/feed?after_id=1054` which maps directly to a high-speed keyset query `WHERE id < 1054 ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20`.

Common Pitfall: Paginating without an ORDER BY clause, causing rows to jump around between pages.

What to Avoid (Unordered Pagination): Because table order is non-deterministic, Page 2 may repeat rows from Page 1 or miss records entirely.

Recommended Fix (Stable Deterministic Pagination): Guarantees that every page contains a distinct, consistent partition of records.

Why It Matters: Stable pagination prevents duplicate or missing items on product catalogues, search results, and admin tables.

Key Takeaways:
- Return Small Pages: Always paginate large tables to conserve bandwidth, memory, and database resources.
- Always Use ORDER BY: Deterministic ordering by unique keys prevents missing or duplicated rows across pages.
- Keyset for Scale: Use keyset cursor pagination (`WHERE id > last_seen`) for deep lists and high performance.

codeBlocks.title: Pagination — Return Data in Small Pages
codeBlocks.code:
-- Simple LIMIT / OFFSET pagination (page 3, 10 items per page)
SELECT id, name
FROM products
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;

-- Keyset pagination (more efficient and stable for large datasets)
SELECT id, name
FROM products
WHERE id > 20
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 10;

codeBlocks.title: Unordered Pagination
codeBlocks.code:
-- Flawed: No ORDER BY!
SELECT id, name FROM products LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;

codeBlocks.title: Stable Deterministic Pagination

lessons.title: Safe Queries and SQL Injection
lessons.subtitle: Protect databases against SQL injection vulnerabilities by utilizing parameterized queries and prepared statements.
lessons.stageName: Work with Data Efficiently and Safely
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Protect your database against SQL injection vulnerabilities by separating SQL syntax from user data using parameterized queries ($1, $2).

Real-World Scenario: A search box sends a user's search text to PostgreSQL. How should the developer pass that text to the query? -> Use a parameterized query. Do not insert the user's text directly into the SQL string.

Big Picture: SQL injection happens when untrusted user input is joined into SQL text in a way that changes the meaning of the query. Use parameterized queries so values are sent separately from the SQL command.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Placeholder syntax ($1, $2): The SQL statement defines positional placeholders (`$1`, `$2`) instead of string interpolations.
- 2. Values parameter array: User inputs are transmitted separately in an array over the PostgreSQL wire protocol.
- 3. Separation of code and data: The PostgreSQL query parser pre-compiles the SQL syntax before binding the parameter values.
- 4. Complete injection immunity: Even if an input contains quotes like `' OR '1'='1`, the database treats it as a literal string value, completely preventing SQL injection.

Core Rule (Parameterized Query Rule): Never concatenate, interpolate, or format untrusted user input directly into SQL query strings. Always use parameterized queries (`$1, $2, ...`) provided by your database driver.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- How Attacks Happen: An attacker inputs `admin' --`. In a concatenated query, `--` comments out the password check, granting unauthorized administrator access.
- Separate Wire Transmission: PostgreSQL protocol transmits the query plan and parameter values in separate protocol packets, guaranteeing the parser treats parameters strictly as data.
- Prepared Statement Caching: Parameterized queries allow PostgreSQL to cache query execution plans across requests, providing a significant performance boost.

In Practice:
- Authentication Queries: Login forms are the #1 target for injection attacks. Using `pool.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', [email])` ensures malicious payloads are treated as literal email strings.
- Search Inputs with Wildcards: When searching with `ILIKE`, pass the wildcards in the parameter array: `pool.query('SELECT * FROM products WHERE name ILIKE $1', ['%' + term + '%'])`.

Common Pitfall: Using JavaScript template literals to construct raw SQL strings from request parameters.

What to Avoid (Vulnerable String Concatenation): An attacker can extract private user records, dump passwords, or drop entire database tables.

Recommended Fix (Parameterized Safe Query): Safely handles any input string, including quotes and control characters, without risk.

Why It Matters: Parameterized queries prevent SQL injection entirely, protecting user credentials, corporate data, and regulatory compliance.

Key Takeaways:
- Separate Code from Data: Never concatenate untrusted user strings directly into SQL text.
- Use $1, $2 Placeholders: Pass inputs in the parameters array using `$1, $2` syntax in Node.js and PostgreSQL drivers.
- Zero-Trust Philosophy: Treat all input from users, webhooks, and third-party APIs as untrusted data.

lessons.title: Database Roles and Permissions
lessons.subtitle: Apply the principle of least privilege using PostgreSQL roles, schemas, and granular GRANT privileges.
lessons.stageName: Work with Data Efficiently and Safely
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Apply the principle of least privilege using PostgreSQL database roles, schemas, and granular GRANT permissions instead of using superusers.

Real-World Scenario: A reporting service only needs to read data. Should it use a database superuser account? -> No. Give it a role with only the permissions it needs, such as permission to connect and read the required tables.

Big Picture: A database role represents a user or a group of permissions. Give each application or person only the access it needs.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. CREATE ROLE ... LOGIN: Creates a new database identity with authentication credentials able to establish client connections.
- 2. GRANT CONNECT: Authorizes the role to connect to the specific `shop` database.
- 3. GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA: Allows the role to look up and reference objects within the `public` schema.
- 4. GRANT SELECT: Grants read-only permission across tables without granting mutation privileges like INSERT, UPDATE, or DROP.

Core Rule (Principle of Least Privilege Rule): Never connect production applications using the `postgres` superuser account. Create dedicated roles for each service and grant only the minimal privileges required (`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`).

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Granular Permissions: Grant specific actions (`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`) only on the specific tables the application service actually uses.
- Reporting Roles: Analytics workers and replica connections should connect using a read-only role (`GRANT SELECT`) to eliminate the risk of accidental writes.
- Restricting DDL: Application runtime users should never have permission to execute DDL (`DROP TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`). Reserve DDL for automated migration pipelines.

In Practice:
- Read-Only Analytics Dashboards: Connecting tools like Metabase or Tableau with `app_reader` guarantees that an analyst's custom SQL query can never accidentally truncate or update a production table.
- Default Privileges for Future Tables: `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO app_reader;` ensures newly created tables automatically inherit read permissions.

Common Pitfall: Connecting web applications and analytics tools using the 'postgres' superuser account.

What to Avoid (Using Superuser Everywhere): Superusers bypass all permissions and row security checks, leaving the entire database vulnerable to catastrophic failure.

Recommended Fix (Dedicated Restricted Application Roles): Safely restricts the application to its designated table operational boundary.

Why It Matters: Role-based access control minimizes damage from compromised credentials, zero-day vulnerabilities, and human error.

Key Takeaways:
- Least Privilege: Give every application role only the minimal permissions it needs to perform its job.
- Never Use Superuser in Apps: Do not connect production applications or analytics tools using the superuser account.
- Roles and Grants: Use `CREATE ROLE` to define identities and `GRANT` to allocate specific table privileges.

lessons.title: Backups and Restoring Data
lessons.subtitle: Protect business data with logical backups using pg_dump, custom format archives, and regular restore drills.
lessons.stageName: Work with Data Efficiently and Safely
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Implement reliable disaster recovery using pg_dump custom format archives and verify data safety through regular automated restore drills.

Real-World Scenario: A team makes backups every day but has never tried restoring one. Is that enough? -> No. The team should test restoring backups regularly. A backup that cannot be restored will not help during an emergency.

Big Picture: A backup is a copy of database data that can be used to recover after data is lost or damaged. A backup is useful only if you can restore it successfully.

A common PostgreSQL logical backup uses `pg_dump` and `pg_restore`.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. pg_dump command: Connects to the database and streams a consistent snapshot without locking reads.
- 2. The -Fc flag: Instructs `pg_dump` to output in PostgreSQL's compressed custom archive format, which supports parallel restoring and table reordering.
- 3. createdb target: Creates a dedicated isolated database to test and verify the restoration.
- 4. pg_restore command: Reads the archive file and reconstructs tables, schema constraints, indexes, and row data.
- 5. Data verification: Always query restored tables to confirm row counts and data integrity before considering a backup valid.

Core Rule (Restore Verification Rule): An unverified backup cannot be relied upon in an outage. Regularly automate backup restoration drills into a test database to prove that recovery works.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- pg_dump Custom Format: Prefer `pg_dump -Fc` over plain text SQL dumps. It is compressed, faster, and allows restoring specific tables selectively with `pg_restore`.
- Zero-Downtime Dumps: `pg_dump` relies on PostgreSQL's MVCC snapshots. It takes a consistent point-in-time backup without blocking concurrent reads or writes.
- Scheduled Recovery Testing: Automate weekly or monthly automated restore scripts that spin up a test database, load the dump, and assert table counts.

In Practice:
- Disaster Recovery Testing: Schedule a monthly cron job that takes last night's dump, restores it to a temporary staging database, and runs automated tests to verify schema and data health.
- Off-Site Storage: Always encrypt and transfer backup archives to off-site, geographically separate object storage (e.g. S3 Glacier) with retention lifecycle policies.

Common Pitfall: Taking daily backups but never testing whether the dump files can actually be restored.

What to Avoid (Untested Backups): Leaves the company with zero recoverable data during a production disaster.

Recommended Fix (Automated Backup & Restore Drill): Guarantees that every backup file is verified as complete, uncorrupted, and 100% restorable.

Why It Matters: A tested backup strategy guarantees business continuity and eliminates catastrophic data loss.

Key Takeaways:
- Backup & Restore Pair: A backup is a recovery copy of database data; a backup is only useful if it can be successfully restored.
- pg_dump & pg_restore: Use `pg_dump -Fc` for compressed custom archives and `pg_restore` to rebuild databases.
- Test Regularly: Regular restore drills prove that your recovery plans and files actually work.

codeBlocks.title: Backups and Restoring Data
codeBlocks.code:
# 1. Create a compressed custom archive backup of the 'shop' database:
pg_dump -Fc -d shop -f shop-backup.dump

# 2. Create a clean test database and restore the backup:
createdb shop_restore_test
pg_restore -d shop_restore_test shop-backup.dump

codeBlocks.code:
# Team sets up daily dump cron job:
0 2 * * * pg_dump shop > /tmp/backup.sql
# But never tests restoring! During a server failure 6 months later,
# they discover disk filled up mid-dump and all backup files are corrupted!

codeBlocks.title: Automated Backup & Restore Drill
codeBlocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
set -e
TIMESTAMP=$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)
# 1. Take compressed custom backup
pg_dump -Fc -d shop -f "/backups/shop_${TIMESTAMP}.dump"

# 2. Automated drill: test restore into temporary database
createdb "restore_test_${TIMESTAMP}"
pg_restore -d "restore_test_${TIMESTAMP}" "/backups/shop_${TIMESTAMP}.dump"
psql -d "restore_test_${TIMESTAMP}" -c "SELECT count(*) FROM orders;"
dropdb "restore_test_${TIMESTAMP}"
echo "Backup and restore drill verified successfully!"

lessons.title: What Is MongoDB?
lessons.subtitle: MongoDB is a database that stores information as documents similar to JavaScript objects.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Discover why MongoDB was created, the core document model concept, and how keeping related data together improves speed and clarity.

Real-World Scenario: You are building a course website. The course title and price must still be available tomorrow. Why would you use MongoDB? -> I can save each course as a document in MongoDB. The data stays in the database, so the application can read it again later.

Big Picture: MongoDB is a database that stores information as documents. A document looks similar to a JavaScript object. This makes it natural to store data such as users, products, courses, and orders.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Document structure: Information is grouped in key-value pairs, just like a JavaScript object.
- 2. Data types: Fields hold familiar types: strings ("JavaScript Basics"), numbers (500), and booleans (true).
- 3. Persistence: MongoDB stores this document permanently on disk so your app can retrieve it anytime.

Core Rule (Persistence & Document Model Rule): Use MongoDB when your application needs to store and query document-shaped data. Choose a database based on the needs of the project; MongoDB is not automatically the best choice for every application.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Persistent Storage: Memory in Node.js resets when the server restarts. MongoDB keeps your records safe on disk.
- Natural Object Shape: Stores documents directly matching the JSON-like objects already used in modern application code.
- Deliberate Database Choice: Evaluate project requirements carefully. MongoDB is ideal for document data, but evaluate relational or cache stores where appropriate.

In Practice:
- Course Catalog Storage: When a platform creates a new course, it sends the course object to MongoDB. The database writes the document to disk and returns a confirmation.
- Surviving Restarts: Even if the Node.js API server crashes or updates to a new version, all courses remain preserved in MongoDB ready to be queried on restart.

Common Pitfall: Relying on in-memory JavaScript variables or global arrays to store user data across requests.

What to Avoid (Storing Data in In-Memory Variables): In-memory arrays disappear the instant your process terminates or crashes, causing catastrophic data loss.

Recommended Fix (Persisting Records in MongoDB): MongoDB writes documents to permanent storage with transaction logging, guaranteeing durability.

Key Takeaways:
- Document Database: MongoDB stores data in JSON-like documents, making it natural to represent application objects.
- Durable Persistence: Data saved in MongoDB survives server restarts, deployments, and page closures.
- Deliberate Tool Selection: Choose MongoDB when document-shaped data and queries fit your project requirements.

lessons.title: Databases, Collections, Documents, and BSON
lessons.subtitle: Organize data hierarchically in databases, collections, and BSON documents with rich types.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Understand MongoDB database hierarchy, collections, ObjectId generation, and how binary JSON (BSON) supports rich types.

Real-World Scenario: A learner has a name, a list of skills, and an address. Can MongoDB store all of these in one document? -> Yes. A document can contain normal fields, arrays, and other documents. This keeps related information together.

Big Picture: MongoDB organizes data in three main levels:

- **Database:** Holds related collections.
- **Collection:** Holds documents of a similar kind. It is roughly like a table in a relational database.
- **Document:** One saved record, written as field-and-value pairs.

Think of a database as a filing cabinet, a collection as a folder, and a document as one file inside that folder.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. name and age: `name` and `age` are simple fields.
- 2. skills array: `skills` is an array because one person can have several skills.
- 3. address embedded document: `address` is a document inside another document. This is called an embedded document.
- 4. _id primary key: `_id` identifies the document. MongoDB creates an `_id` automatically when you do not provide one.

Core Rule (Three-Tier Organization Rule): Databases contain collections, collections contain documents, and documents contain typed fields and values stored in BSON binary format.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Filing Cabinet Analogy: Database = filing cabinet. Collection = folder. Document = individual file inside that folder.
- Binary JSON (BSON): Extends JSON with high-performance binary encoding and native types like ObjectId, Date, and 64-bit integers.
- Automatic _id: Every document requires an `_id`. MongoDB generates a unique 12-byte ObjectId if you don't supply one.

In Practice:
- Unified Student Record: In relational databases, storing Rina's skills and address would require 3 tables and foreign keys. In MongoDB, it is stored cleanly in a single document.
- BSON Serialization: When you query MongoDB, the driver converts BSON bytes back into native JavaScript objects seamlessly.

Common Pitfall: Confusing MongoDB collections with relational tables or treating documents as plain strings without types.

What to Avoid (Storing Nested Information as Stringified JSON): MongoDB cannot query or index fields inside a raw string without parsing the entire string.

Recommended Fix (Storing Nested Structures as Embedded Documents): Embedded documents preserve native BSON types and allow precise dot notation querying like address.city.

Key Takeaways:
- Three Levels of Data: Database -> Collection -> Document represents the core MongoDB storage structure.
- Rich BSON Types: BSON provides support for native ObjectIds, dates, embedded subdocuments, and arrays.
- Colocated Information: Embedding related attributes together avoids complex joins for natural entity structures.

lessons.title: Working with MongoDB Using mongosh
lessons.subtitle: Use the interactive MongoDB Shell (mongosh) and MongoDB Compass to manage databases and collections.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Learn practical commands in mongosh (use, show dbs, show collections) and visually inspect documents with MongoDB Compass.

Real-World Scenario: You ran `use learncraft`, but the database does not appear in `show dbs`. Did the command fail? -> Not necessarily. Selecting a database does not create stored data. MongoDB normally shows the database after data has been written to it.

Big Picture: `mongosh` is a command-line tool for working with MongoDB. You can use it to select a database, view collections, and run queries.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. show dbs: `show dbs` lists databases that contain data.
- 2. use learncraft: `use learncraft` switches the shell to the `learncraft` database. It does not necessarily create the database immediately.
- 3. show collections: `show collections` lists the collections in the selected database.
- 4. db.courses.find(): `db.courses.find()` reads documents from the `courses` collection.

Core Rule (Lazy Creation Rule): MongoDB defers physical allocation of databases and collections on disk until the first document is actually inserted.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- mongosh Interactive Shell: Full Node.js-powered REPL shell for querying, administering, and scripting database operations.
- MongoDB Compass: Official GUI tool for visual document inspection, schema analysis, and index visualization.
- On-Demand Creation: Databases and collections spring into existence the moment you insert your first document.

In Practice:
- Switching Databases: Running `use learncraft` sets the shell's active context pointer (`db`). Future collection references like `db.courses` point directly to that database.
- Empty Database Behavior: If a database has 0 collections or 0 documents, `show dbs` omits it by design to save storage and keep the listing clean.

Common Pitfall: Panicking when an empty database does not show up in `show dbs` immediately after `use <dbname>`.

What to Avoid (Assuming Database Creation Failed): MongoDB does not allocate files for empty databases until you write at least one record.

Recommended Fix (Writing a First Document to Persist Database): Once a write operation occurs, MongoDB allocates the namespace on disk and displays it in `show dbs`.

Key Takeaways:
- mongosh Navigation: Use `show dbs`, `use <dbname>`, `show collections`, and `db.<collection>.find()` for standard shell workflow.
- Lazy Namespace Allocation: Databases and collections are created on-demand as soon as the first document is inserted.
- Developer Tool Options: Use `mongosh` for fast terminal queries and scripts, or MongoDB Compass for visual exploration.

lessons.title: Insert Documents
lessons.subtitle: Save single or multiple documents into a collection using insertOne() and insertMany().
lessons.stageName: Create, Find, Change, and Delete Data
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Insert single and batch documents into collections, examine the write acknowledgement response, and handle auto-generated _id keys.

Real-World Scenario: An admin adds a new course to the website. Which operation saves it in MongoDB? -> Use `insertOne()` because the admin is adding one course document.

Big Picture: To save a new document, use `insertOne()`. To save several documents at once, use `insertMany()`.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Select collection: `db.courses` selects the `courses` collection.
- 2. Tell MongoDB to save: `insertOne()` tells MongoDB to save one document.
- 3. Fields and values: The object contains the fields and values to save.
- 4. Auto-generated _id: MongoDB adds an `_id` if the document does not already have one.

Core Rule (Document Insertion Rule): Pass a single document object to `insertOne()` and an array of document objects to `insertMany()`. MongoDB returns acknowledgment with the inserted `_id` values.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- insertOne(): Saves one document. Returns `{ acknowledged: true, insertedId: ObjectId(...) }`.
- insertMany(): Accepts an array of documents to insert in a single network round-trip, improving batch performance.
- Automatic ID Generation: If omitted, MongoDB automatically generates a unique 12-byte BSON `_id` for every document.

In Practice:
- Admin Dashboard Course Creation: When an instructor submits the 'Create Course' form, the server calls `insertOne()` with the title, price, and status.
- Data Seeding & Migrations: When initializing a test database or importing initial catalog records, using `insertMany([...])` is much faster than looping `insertOne()`.

Common Pitfall: Passing a single object directly into `insertMany()` or passing an array into `insertOne()`.

What to Avoid (Passing Array to insertOne()): insertOne() expects a single document object, not an array.

Recommended Fix (Using the Correct Method for the Structure): insertMany() cleanly accepts an array of documents and inserts each one individually.

Key Takeaways:
- insertOne(): Inserts a single document and automatically generates an `_id` if omitted.
- insertMany(): Inserts an array of documents in a single efficient batch operation.
- Write Acknowledgment: MongoDB confirms each write with status and inserted identifiers.

lessons.title: Find Documents
lessons.subtitle: Query documents from a collection using find() for multiple results and findOne() for single matches.
lessons.stageName: Create, Find, Change, and Delete Data
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Retrieve documents matching criteria and shape network payloads with projection to return only requested fields.

Real-World Scenario: A course details page needs to show one course using its title. Which method can you use? -> Use `findOne()` with a title filter because the page needs one matching course.

Big Picture: Use `find()` to read documents from a collection. Use `findOne()` when you only need one matching document.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. The query filter: The object inside `findOne()` is the filter.
- 2. Matching evaluation: MongoDB looks for a document whose `title` is `React Basics`.
- 3. Result returned: It returns one matching document, or `null` when no document matches.

Core Rule (Query Method Selection Rule): `find()` returns a cursor pointing to multiple documents, whereas `findOne()` returns the single document object or null directly.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- db.collection.find(): Returns a cursor to iterate over matching documents. An empty filter `{}` matches all documents.
- db.collection.findOne(): Returns the first matching document found on disk, or null if no document matches the filter criteria.
- Filter Object: Specify field-value pairs to restrict which documents are selected from storage.

In Practice:
- Course Catalog Listing: The `/courses` index page calls `db.courses.find()` to display a list of all available offerings.
- Single Course Details Page: The `/courses/:title` route calls `db.courses.findOne({ title })` to render that specific course's description and pricing.

Common Pitfall: Using `find()` when your application expects a single document object, causing array/cursor mismatch bugs.

What to Avoid (Calling find() When Expecting an Object): find() returns a cursor over a set of documents. To get a single document directly, use findOne().

Recommended Fix (Using findOne() for Single Document Lookups): findOne() directly resolves to the document or null, avoiding unnecessary array indexing.

Key Takeaways:
- find(): Returns a cursor over all documents matching the filter.
- findOne(): Returns a single document or null if no document matches.
- Filter Objects: Pass key-value objects like `{ title: 'React Basics' }` to find matching documents.

lessons.title: Filter Documents with Query Operators
lessons.subtitle: Filter collections using comparison ($gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $in) and logical operators ($and, $or).
lessons.stageName: Create, Find, Change, and Delete Data
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Filter documents with precision using comparison, logical, element, and regex operators alongside sorting and pagination.

Real-World Scenario: A learner wants to see published courses that cost less than 1,000. How can you find them? -> Use a filter with `isPublished: true` and `price: { $lt: 1000 }`. MongoDB returns courses that meet both conditions.

Big Picture: A filter tells MongoDB which documents you want. Query operators let you search using conditions instead of exact matches only.

Example: find courses that cost at least 500.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. The field to check: `price` is the field MongoDB checks.
- 2. The operator $gte: `$gte` means "greater than or equal to".
- 3. Results matched: MongoDB returns documents where `price` is 500 or more.
- 4. Implicit AND: When you put multiple fields in one filter object, MongoDB applies an AND condition: all those conditions must match.

Core Rule (Query Operator Syntax Rule): Field-level comparison operators take the shape `{ field: { $operator: value } }`. Compound conditions use `{ $and: [...] }` or `{ $or: [...] }`.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- $gt / $gte / $lt / $lte: Greater than ($gt), greater or equal ($gte), less than ($lt), less or equal ($lte) for numbers and dates.
- $in & $ne: `$in` matches any value in a list (e.g. `{ category: { $in: ['web', 'backend'] } }`). `$ne` matches not equal.
- $and & $or: `$or` matches if at least one condition is true. Multiple fields in an object apply implicit `$and`.

In Practice:
- Budget Pricing Filter: Filtering for affordable courses: `db.courses.find({ price: { $gte: 200, $lte: 800 } })` finds records between 200 and 800 inclusive.
- Multi-Category Search: Finding courses in multiple categories: `db.courses.find({ category: { $in: ['javascript', 'database'] } })` efficiently queries across categories.

Common Pitfall: Forgetting the `$` prefix on operators or using JavaScript comparison operators like `>=` instead of `$gte`.

What to Avoid (Using Raw JavaScript Comparison Operators): MongoDB query filters are plain BSON objects and require operators like `$gte`.

Recommended Fix (Using MongoDB Query Operators): `{ price: { $gte: 500 } }` correctly instructs the query engine to evaluate the condition.

Key Takeaways:
- Comparison Operators: Use `$gt`, `$gte`, `$lt`, `$lte`, and `$ne` to compare values.
- List Membership with $in: Use `{ field: { $in: [...] } }` to match any value in a list.
- Implicit AND: Multiple fields within the same filter object must all match by default.

lessons.title: Choose Fields, Sort Results, and Limit Results
lessons.subtitle: Optimize query payloads using projections (1/0), sorting (1/-1), and result limiting.
lessons.stageName: Create, Find, Change, and Delete Data
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Shape query results with field projections (inclusion and exclusion), ascending and descending sorts, and result limits.

Real-World Scenario: A course list should show only the course title and price, with the cheapest courses first. What should you use? -> Use projection to select the title and price, then sort by price in ascending order.

Big Picture: Sometimes you do not need every field or every document. MongoDB lets you choose fields, sort results, and limit the number of results.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Projection argument: The second argument to `find()` is the projection. `1` includes a field and `0` excludes it. MongoDB includes `_id` by default, so `_id: 0` explicitly hides it.
- 2. sort({ field: 1 / -1 }): `1` sorts from low to high. `-1` sorts from high to low.
- 3. limit(n): Restricts the cursor to return at most `n` documents.

Core Rule (Payload & Cursor Shaping Rule): Never transfer unneeded fields over the network. Always apply projections to minimize bandwidth and memory usage, and combine with explicit sort and limit.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Projection (1 and 0): Pick exact fields to return. You cannot mix 1 and 0 in the same projection, except for suppressing `_id: 0`.
- Sorting Direction: `1` specifies ascending (lowest first, A-Z), `-1` specifies descending (highest first, Z-A).
- Limiting Count: `limit(5)` caps the returned documents, preventing queries from accidentally returning hundreds of thousands of records.

In Practice:
- Cheapest Courses Widget: A homepage carousel displays the 5 cheapest courses: `db.courses.find({}, { title: 1, price: 1 }).sort({ price: 1 }).limit(5)` fetches exactly what's needed.
- Omitting Large Binary or Text Fields: If course documents contain full lesson transcripts or large embedded metadata, project `{ transcript: 0 }` so summary cards load rapidly.

Common Pitfall: Mixing 1 and 0 in a projection object (e.g. `{ title: 1, description: 0 }`), which triggers a MongoDB projection error.

What to Avoid (Mixing Inclusion and Exclusion (except _id)): MongoDB projections must be either entirely inclusive (1s) or entirely exclusive (0s), with the sole exception of `_id: 0`.

Recommended Fix (Using Pure Inclusion with Optional _id Suppression): This cleanly returns only `title` and `price`, omitting `_id` and all other fields.

Key Takeaways:
- Projection: Use `{ field: 1 }` to include or `{ field: 0 }` to exclude fields. `_id` is included unless explicitly set to 0.
- Sorting: Use `.sort({ field: 1 })` for ascending or `.sort({ field: -1 })` for descending order.
- Limiting: Use `.limit(n)` to cap response payloads to a specific maximum count.

lessons.title: Update Documents
lessons.subtitle: Modify documents atomically using updateOne(), updateMany(), $set, $unset, and $inc.
lessons.stageName: Create, Find, Change, and Delete Data
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Perform atomic in-place updates using $set, modify counters with $inc, remove fields with $unset, and avoid full document replacement.

Real-World Scenario: A course price changes, but its title and description must stay the same. How should you update it? -> Use `updateOne()` with a filter that identifies the course and `$set` only the price field. The other fields remain unchanged.

Big Picture: Use `updateOne()` to change one matching document and `updateMany()` to change all matching documents.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Match filter: The first object finds the course to change.
- 2. The $set operator: `$set` changes the `price` field to `750`.
- 3. Unaltered fields: Other fields stay as they are.
- 4. The $inc operator: `$inc` increments or decrements numeric values atomically without race conditions.

Core Rule (Targeted Field Update Rule): Always use atomic update operators like `$set` or `$inc` to update fields in-place. An update filter matters: check it carefully so you do not change the wrong documents.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- $set & $unset: `$set` updates or creates specified fields. `$unset` completely removes a field from matching documents.
- $inc Counters: Increases or decreases numbers atomically. E.g. `{ $inc: { views: 1 } }` or `{ $inc: { stock: -1 } }`.
- $push & $addToSet: `$push` appends an item to an array. `$addToSet` appends an item only if it does not already exist.

In Practice:
- Course Enrollment Counter: When a student buys a course, running `db.courses.updateOne({ _id: courseId }, { $inc: { enrolledCount: 1 } })` ensures the count is accurate even under concurrent purchases.
- Bulk Price Adjustment: Applying a sale across a category: `db.courses.updateMany({ category: 'web' }, { $set: { onSale: true } })` updates all matching documents in one operation.

Common Pitfall: Forgetting the `$set` operator in update methods or calling `replaceOne()` accidentally, wiping out all other fields in the document.

What to Avoid (Accidental Document Overwrite): Full document replacement wipes out all unmentioned fields, keeping only `price` and the original `_id`.

Recommended Fix (In-Place Field Update with $set): `$set` changes only the specified fields, preserving all existing document attributes.

Key Takeaways:
- In-Place $set: Use `$set` to add or update specific fields while preserving all other document data.
- Atomic $inc: Use `$inc` to safely increment or decrement numeric counters without race conditions.
- Careful Filtering: Always verify your query filter before executing `updateMany()` to avoid unintended changes.
