lessons.title: Delete Documents Safely
lessons.subtitle: Remove documents with deleteOne() and deleteMany() while preventing accidental mass deletion.
lessons.stageName: Create, Find, Change, and Delete Data
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Remove specific documents or multiple records safely using query filters, inspect deletedCount, and implement soft delete flags.

Real-World Scenario: An admin wants to remove one discontinued course. What should they do? -> Use `deleteOne()` with a filter that identifies that course. Check the filter before running the command.

Big Picture: Use `deleteOne()` to remove one matching document and `deleteMany()` to remove all matching documents.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Filter evaluation: MongoDB checks the filter.
- 2. Removal of match: It removes one matching document.
- 3. Result response: It reports how many documents were deleted (e.g. `{ acknowledged: true, deletedCount: 1 }`).
- 4. Empty filter warning: `deleteMany({})` removes every document in the collection. Do not run it unless deleting all records is truly intended.

Core Rule (Deletion Safeguard Rule): Never run `deleteMany()` without an explicit, validated filter. Verify the target document count with `find(filter).count()` before running destructive operations.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- deleteOne(): Finds the first document matching the query criteria and permanently removes it from the collection.
- deleteMany(): Deletes all documents that match the provided filter. Passing `{}` removes all records.
- Soft Delete Pattern: Instead of physically deleting, set `{ isDeleted: true, deletedAt: new Date() }` to allow recovery and auditing.

In Practice:
- Removing Discontinued Course: When an admin archives a single course: `db.courses.deleteOne({ _id: courseId })` targets the unique ID to ensure only that one course is deleted.
- Clearing Expired Sessions: A periodic maintenance task deletes old sessions: `db.sessions.deleteMany({ expiresAt: { $lt: new Date() } })` cleans up only expired records.

Common Pitfall: Accidentally running `deleteMany({})` or passing an undefined variable as a filter, wiping out the entire collection.

What to Avoid (Running deleteMany() with Empty Filter): An empty or unvalidated filter in `deleteMany` destroys every single document in the collection.

Recommended Fix (Validating Filter Before Deletion): Validating inputs ensures deletion is strictly targeted to the intended document.

Key Takeaways:
- deleteOne(): Removes a single document matching the specified filter criteria.
- deleteMany() Caution: Never pass an empty filter `{}` to `deleteMany()` unless you genuinely intend to truncate the collection.
- Filter Verification: Double-check your filter and test query counts with `find()` prior to deleting.

lessons.title: Arrays and Embedded Documents
lessons.subtitle: Organize related data within documents using arrays and embedded subdocuments with dot notation.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Query sub-documents with dot notation and manipulate array fields cleanly using $push, $pull, $addToSet, and positional operators.

Real-World Scenario: A course always displays its instructor's name and city. How could you store that information together? -> Store an `instructor` object inside the course document. Then the course and instructor details can be read together.

Big Picture: A MongoDB document can contain an array or another document. This lets you keep related information together.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Array matching: `tags` contains an array, so MongoDB can match a value inside that array directly.
- 2. Embedded document: `instructor` is a document inside the course document.
- 3. Dot notation: Dot notation, such as `"instructor.city"`, lets you search a field inside the embedded document.

Core Rule (Data Colocation Rule): Embed data that is strictly bounded in size and always queried alongside its parent. Use quoted dot notation `"parent.field"` for querying and updating nested properties.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Array Fields: Store lists of scalar values or lists of objects (e.g. tags, roles, variants). Queried directly without special syntax.
- Embedded Subdocuments: Nested objects grouped under a parent key. Keep related attributes like addresses or author profiles together.
- Quoted Dot Notation: Always wrap nested paths in quotes (e.g. `"address.city": "Dhaka"`) when filtering or updating.

In Practice:
- Course Tags Filtering: Finding courses tagged with 'backend': `db.courses.find({ tags: 'backend' })` automatically scans elements inside the `tags` array without requiring an explicit `$elemMatch` for simple scalar checks.
- Instructor Information Colocation: When viewing a course, displaying the instructor's name and city doesn't require a second database query or join because it is embedded inside the course document.

Common Pitfall: Forgetting quotes around dot notation keys in query filters, causing JavaScript syntax errors.

What to Avoid (Unquoted Dot Notation in Query): In JavaScript object literals, property keys containing dots must be wrapped in quotes.

Recommended Fix (Quoted Dot Notation Path): Wrapping `"instructor.city"` in quotes tells MongoDB to traverse the nested object path correctly.

Key Takeaways:
- Arrays in Documents: MongoDB natively supports arrays and matches elements directly in query filters.
- Embedded Subdocuments: Store related attributes inside the parent document to eliminate unnecessary queries.
- Quoted Dot Notation: Use `"parent.child"` syntax with quotes to query and update nested properties.

lessons.title: Embedding vs. Referencing Related Data
lessons.subtitle: Choose between embedded documents (denormalization) and referenced ObjectId links (normalization).
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Model real-world relationships by understanding when to embed vs when to reference based on access patterns and document size limits.

Real-World Scenario: A course page always shows a small instructor summary. Should you embed the instructor summary or reference a separate instructor document? -> Embedding a small summary can work well because the page reads it with the course. If the full instructor record is shared and updated separately by many courses, use a reference instead.

Big Picture: When two kinds of data are related, you need to decide whether to put them in one document or keep them in separate documents and link them.

There is no rule that every relationship must use embedding or every relationship must use references. MongoDB data modeling should follow how the application uses the data.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Read together: Ask whether the data is usually read together.
- 2. Size and containment: Ask whether the related data is small and belongs naturally to its parent.
- 3. Shared entities: Ask whether many documents need to share the same related record.
- 4. Frequency of change: Consider how often each piece of data changes.
- 5. Workload alignment: Choose the structure that fits the application's common queries and updates.

Core Rule (Data Modeling Decision Rule): Embed when data is 1-to-few, bounded in size, and read together. Reference when relationships are unbounded 1-to-many, frequently mutated by independent workflows, or shared across multiple collections.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- When to Embed: Small sub-records, read alongside parent, 1-to-few, and updated atomically in a single write operation.
- When to Reference: Shared entities (e.g. instructors), unbounded growth (e.g. comments, logs), or records mutated frequently on their own.
- 16MB Document Limit: MongoDB enforces a maximum size of 16MB per BSON document. Unbounded embedding will eventually fail.

In Practice:
- Course with Instructor Summary: A course card embeds `{ instructorName: 'Rina', avatarUrl: '...' }` to render the catalog instantly without joining, but references `instructorId` for the full bio and payroll records.
- Order Items Snapshot: Orders embed the line items and price at the exact moment of purchase so future price adjustments never alter historical order receipts.

Common Pitfall: Embedding an unbounded array of reviews, comments, or log entries directly inside a parent document, eventually exceeding the 16MB document limit.

What to Avoid (Unbounded Array Growth Inside a Single Document): Every write rewrites the whole growing document on disk, causing memory fragmentation and eventual crash at 16MB.

Recommended Fix (Referencing Unbounded 1-to-Many Relationships): Each review is an independent document with no upper limit on the total number of reviews.

Key Takeaways:
- Embedding for Locality: Colocate bounded 1-to-few data that is always accessed together for fast single-seek disk reads.
- Referencing for Scalability: Use references for unbounded relationships, shared entities, and independently mutating records.
- Application-Driven Modeling: Model data based on your application's actual read and write queries, not rigid theoretical rules.

lessons.title: Schema Validation
lessons.subtitle: Enforce collection integrity, required keys, and BSON type checks with $jsonSchema validation rules.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Harness flexible schemas safely by enforcing collection-level rules with $jsonSchema, required fields, and validation actions.

Real-World Scenario: Someone tries to save a course with a price of `"free"` instead of a number. How can MongoDB help prevent this? -> Add schema validation that requires `price` to be a number. MongoDB can reject a document that does not follow the rule.

Big Picture: MongoDB has a flexible data model, but flexible does not mean every document should contain random or incorrect values. **Schema validation** lets you define rules for the documents in a collection.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. validator object: `validator` contains the rules for documents in the collection.
- 2. required array: `required` says that `title` and `price` must exist.
- 3. bsonType check: `bsonType` checks the kind of value (e.g. "string", "number", "object").
- 4. Constraints (minimum: 0): `minimum: 0` prevents a negative price.

Core Rule (Defense in Depth Rule): Validate inputs in your application layer (e.g. Zod or Joi) and enforce rules at the database level with `$jsonSchema`. Database schema validation acts as the ultimate safety net against bugs and rogue scripts.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Database Safety Net: Rejects malformed writes at the database layer before corrupted records can compromise production data.
- $jsonSchema Standard: Uses the industry-standard JSON Schema specification extended with BSON type validation (`bsonType`).
- App Validation Synergy: Database validation complements application input checks rather than replacing them.

In Practice:
- Preventing String Prices: If a frontend form sends `{ price: 'free' }`, MongoDB throws a `DocumentValidationFailure` and blocks the write because the schema expects a number with `minimum: 0`.
- Enforcing Mandatory User Fields: Ensuring every user document in `users` has `email` and `createdAt` before any write can be acknowledged.

Common Pitfall: Relying solely on frontend validation and having no validation rules on the collection, allowing direct mongosh or API script errors to write corrupt records.

What to Avoid (Zero Database Validation Rules): Without schema validation, MongoDB permits arbitrary types and shapes, allowing corrupted records into production.

Recommended Fix (Enforcing Types and Ranges with $jsonSchema): MongoDB automatically rejects writes that do not adhere to the `$jsonSchema` specification.

Key Takeaways:
- $jsonSchema Validation: Define collection rules using JSON Schema with BSON type checks.
- Required Fields: Specify arrays of mandatory keys with the `required` constraint.
- Defense in Depth: Pair application-level validation with database-level schema enforcement.

lessons.title: Indexes
lessons.subtitle: Accelerate query performance with single-field, compound, and unique indexes while managing write costs.
lessons.stageName: Find and Work with Data Efficiently
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Accelerate reads and prevent full collection scans using single-field, compound, and unique indexes guided by query patterns.

Real-World Scenario: A products page becomes slow when users search by product name. What could help? -> An index on the product name may help. First check the query and use `explain()` to see whether MongoDB is scanning too many documents.

Big Picture: An index helps MongoDB find documents faster. Without a useful index, MongoDB may need to examine many documents to answer a query.

Think of an index like the index at the back of a book. Instead of checking every page, you use the index to find where a topic appears.

Suppose your application often searches courses by `title`:

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Search pattern: Your application often searches by `title`.
- 2. Index creation: You create an index on the `title` field.
- 3. Index data structure: MongoDB stores extra index information to help locate matching documents.
- 4. Index lookup: A suitable query can use that index instead of examining every document.

Core Rule (Query-Driven Indexing Rule): Index fields based on frequent query filters and sort criteria. Every additional index incurs RAM overhead and write latency on inserts and updates.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Read Acceleration: Changes query execution from an O(N) collection scan (COLLSCAN) to an O(log N) index scan (IXSCAN).
- Write & RAM Overhead: Indexes must fit into Working Set RAM. Every insert, update, or delete must update every index on the collection.
- Prudent Creation: Index only verified query paths. Verify efficiency using `explain()` rather than guessing.

In Practice:
- Product Search Acceleration: In an online catalog with 500,000 items, searching by `productName` without an index examines all 500,000 records. An index on `{ productName: 1 }` resolves the query in a few milliseconds.
- Unique Email Constraint: `db.users.createIndex({ email: 1 }, { unique: true })` both speeds up user login lookups and enforces duplicate email prevention at the database level.

Common Pitfall: Creating an index on every single field in a collection, bloating disk and memory usage and degrading write throughput.

What to Avoid (Over-Indexing Every Property): Every write operation must synchronously update 5 separate B-tree index structures, dramatically slowing down inserts and consuming unnecessary RAM.

Recommended Fix (Targeting Only Query Patterns): Create indexes strictly for fields involved in high-frequency queries and sorting operations.

Key Takeaways:
- Index Purpose: Indexes allow MongoDB to locate documents quickly without scanning every document in the collection.
- Trade-offs: Faster reads come at the cost of additional storage and slower write operations.
- Targeted Indexing: Create indexes that match real application query patterns and verify their usage with `explain()`.

lessons.title: Check a Query with explain()
lessons.subtitle: Diagnose query performance with executionStats, comparing COLLSCAN vs IXSCAN and totalDocsExamined.
lessons.stageName: Find and Work with Data Efficiently
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Profile queries with explain('executionStats'), compare COLLSCAN vs IXSCAN, and verify winning plans.

Real-World Scenario: A query returns 10 courses but examines 50,000 documents. What should you investigate? -> Check the filter and its indexes. Use `explain()` to understand why so many documents are examined, then test a suitable index or query change.

Big Picture: A query may be slow because MongoDB examines too many documents or cannot use a helpful index. `explain()` shows how MongoDB plans and runs a query.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. COLLSCAN: MongoDB scans documents in the collection.
- 2. IXSCAN: MongoDB scans an index.
- 3. totalDocsExamined: How many documents MongoDB examined.
- 4. nReturned: How many documents the query returned.

Core Rule (Query Diagnostics Rule): Run `explain('executionStats')`. Compare `totalDocsExamined` with `nReturned`. When `totalDocsExamined` vastly exceeds `nReturned`, add or adjust indexes to achieve an IXSCAN stage.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- COLLSCAN vs IXSCAN: COLLSCAN inspects every document in storage. IXSCAN uses an indexed B-tree to jump directly to matching pointer records.
- Selectivity Ratio: Ideal ratio of `totalDocsExamined : nReturned` is close to 1:1. High disparity indicates unindexed filtering.
- Workload Context: For collections with only 50 documents, a COLLSCAN is often faster than reading an index from RAM.

In Practice:
- Diagnosing 50,000 Document Scans: When a query for 10 users takes 400ms, running `.explain('executionStats')` reveals `stage: 'COLLSCAN'` and `totalDocsExamined: 50000`. Adding an index drops docs examined to 10.
- Verifying Index Usage: After creating an index, running `explain()` confirms whether the query optimizer selected your index (`winningPlan.inputStage.indexName`).

Common Pitfall: Guessing why a query is slow without checking the execution plan, or assuming every COLLSCAN is automatically a critical defect.

What to Avoid (Guessing Index Strategy Without Profiling): Without running `explain()`, you cannot see which index was chosen or where execution time was spent.

Recommended Fix (Inspecting executionStats with explain()): `executionStats` reveals exact document examination counts and winning plan stages.

Key Takeaways:
- explain('executionStats'): Provides detailed metrics on query planning, winning plans, and execution times.
- COLLSCAN vs IXSCAN: `COLLSCAN` scans all collection documents; `IXSCAN` leverages an index.
- Docs Examined vs Returned: Aim for a ratio where `totalDocsExamined` is as close as possible to `nReturned`.

db.courses
  .find({ title: "React Basics" })
  .explain("executionStats")

lessons.title: Pagination
lessons.subtitle: Paginate large result sets with skip() / limit() and high-performance range-based keyset pagination.
lessons.stageName: Find and Work with Data Efficiently
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Implement reliable pagination using skip() and limit(), and scale large datasets using range-based keyset queries.

Real-World Scenario: Your admin page has thousands of courses. Should it load every course at once? -> No. It should load a small page of courses at a time. For very large result sets, range-based pagination can be more efficient than skipping many documents.

Big Picture: Pagination means returning a large list in smaller groups instead of sending every document at once.

For a simple page-number approach, use `skip()` and `limit()`:

For very large collections, range-based pagination using the last seen ID is significantly faster.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Stable sort order: `sort({ _id: 1 })` gives the results a consistent order.
- 2. skip(20): `skip(20)` skips the first 20 documents.
- 3. limit(10): `limit(10)` returns the next 10 documents.
- 4. Range-based indexing: `{ _id: { $gt: lastSeenId } }` jumps directly past earlier results without having to traverse discarded records.

Core Rule (Pagination Architecture Rule): Use `skip()` and `limit()` for small collections and direct page jumping. Switch to range-based (keyset) pagination `{ field: { $gt: lastSeen } }` when scaling past thousands of documents or infinite scrolling.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- skip() + limit(): Simple to implement. Supports direct page jumping ('Go to page 5'). Becomes linear O(N) as offset increases.
- Range-Based Keyset: Constant O(1) indexed jump using `{ _id: { $gt: lastSeenId } }`. Ideal for infinite feeds and large catalogs.
- Deterministic Sort: Always sort by a unique key (such as `_id`) to ensure documents never appear duplicated or missed across page boundaries.

In Practice:
- E-Commerce Catalog Pages: A store catalog displaying 24 items per page calculates `skip: (page - 1) * 24` and `limit: 24`, allowing buyers to jump directly to page 3.
- Social Activity Feed: Infinite scrolling feeds send the `lastSeenId` from the bottom of the feed: `{ _id: { $lt: oldestSeenId } }` grabs the next chunk instantly.

Common Pitfall: Skipping hundreds of thousands of documents using `skip(500000)`, causing MongoDB to scan all half-million records before returning 10.

What to Avoid (Massive skip() on Large Collections): Large skips force MongoDB to read and discard hundreds of thousands of entries, creating high latency.

Recommended Fix (Range-Based Seek with Index): The B-tree index navigates directly to `lastSeenTimestamp` in O(log N) time, ignoring earlier documents entirely.

Key Takeaways:
- skip() and limit(): Ideal for smaller datasets and traditional page-numbered user interfaces.
- Range-Based Keyset: Use `{ field: { $gt: lastSeen } }` for large collections and infinite scroll patterns.
- Stable Sort Keys: Always pair pagination with a deterministic sort (e.g. `{ _id: 1 }`).

codeBlocks.title: Pagination
codeBlocks.code:
// Approach 1: Offset pagination with skip() & limit() (illustrative):
db.courses
  .find()
  .sort({ _id: 1 })
  .skip(20)
  .limit(10)

// Approach 2: Range-based pagination using last seen ID:
db.courses
  .find({ _id: { $gt: lastSeenId } })
  .sort({ _id: 1 })
  .limit(10)

codeBlocks.title: Massive skip() on Large Collections
Range-Based Seek with Index
codeBlocks.code:
// Fast seek using last timestamp / ID:
db.logs
  .find({ createdAt: { $lt: lastSeenTimestamp } })
  .sort({ createdAt: -1 })
  .limit(20); // Jumps directly via B-tree index!

lessons.title: Aggregation Pipeline
lessons.subtitle: Transform, group, aggregate, and calculate analytical insights through multi-stage pipelines.
lessons.stageName: Find and Work with Data Efficiently
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Transform, group, unwind, and aggregate collections using multi-stage pipelines ($match, $group, $sort, $project).

Real-World Scenario: A shop owner wants to see total sales for each product category. What MongoDB feature can help? -> Use an aggregation pipeline. Filter the orders if needed, group them by category, and use `$sum` to calculate total sales.

Big Picture: An aggregation pipeline processes documents in stages. Each stage receives documents, does one job, and passes its results to the next stage.

For example, imagine an `orders` collection. You want to find how much each customer has spent on paid orders.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. $match: `$match`: Keeps only orders where `status` is `paid`.
- 2. $group: `$group`: Groups those orders by `customerId`.
- 3. $sum: `$sum`: Adds the `amount` values for each customer.
- 4. $sort: `$sort`: Places customers with the highest total first. `-1` means descending order.

Core Rule (Assembly Line Pipeline Rule): Think of aggregation as an assembly line: each stage receives documents, transforms or reduces them, and streams the output to the next stage. Place `$match` as early as possible to reduce document volume before grouping.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- $match Stage: Filters documents early using standard query operators so subsequent stages process fewer documents.
- $group Stage: Groups documents by a key (`_id: '$field'`) and computes accumulator metrics like `$sum`, `$avg`, `$min`, `$max`.
- $project & $sort: Reshapes output fields and orders the resulting computed documents without altering source data.

In Practice:
- Sales by Product Category: Filtering paid orders and grouping by category: `{ $group: { _id: '$category', totalSales: { $sum: '$price' }, count: { $sum: 1 } } }` generates executive dashboards.
- Customer Lifetime Value: Calculating total spend per user and sorting descending gives the top spending VIP customers immediately.

Common Pitfall: Placing `$group` before `$match`, forcing the database to group the entire collection in memory before filtering.

What to Avoid (Grouping Before Matching): Processing unneeded documents in `$group` exhausts memory limits and degrades query speed.

Recommended Fix (Filtering Early with $match): Early `$match` allows MongoDB to use indexes and minimizes the volume of documents piped to memory-intensive stages.

Key Takeaways:
- Stage Pipeline Model: Documents stream through sequential stages like `$match`, `$group`, `$sort`, and `$project`.
- Early Filtering: Place `$match` stages as early as possible to leverage indexes and reduce working set memory.
- Calculated Analytics: Pipelines calculate totals, averages, and group metrics without mutating original stored documents.

lessons.title: Combine Data with $lookup
lessons.subtitle: Join documents across collections within aggregation pipelines using $lookup stages.
lessons.stageName: Find and Work with Data Efficiently
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Join documents across separate collections within aggregation pipelines using indexed $lookup stages.

Real-World Scenario: An order list needs to show the customer's name, but customer details are stored separately. What can you use? -> Use `$lookup` to match each order's `customerId` with the customer's `_id` and include the matching customer data in the result.

Big Picture: Sometimes related information is stored in separate collections. `$lookup` lets an aggregation pipeline match documents from another collection, similar to a join.

Suppose `orders` documents contain a `customerId`, while customer details are stored in a `customers` collection.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. from: `from` names the collection to search: `"customers"`.
- 2. localField: `localField` is the field in the current order document (`"customerId"`).
- 3. foreignField: `foreignField` is the matching field in the customer document (`"_id"`).
- 4. as: `as` names the new field that will contain the matches (`"customer"`).
- 5. Result array: The result includes a `customer` array with matching customer documents.

Core Rule (Prudent Join Rule): Index the `foreignField` in the target collection to ensure `$lookup` stages perform indexed joins rather than full collection scans. Prefer embedding for data that is always accessed together.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Left Outer Join: `$lookup` behaves like an SQL LEFT OUTER JOIN: documents without matches receive an empty array `[]` in the `as` field.
- Foreign Field Index: The collection named in `from` MUST have an index on `foreignField` to avoid O(N × M) nested scan overhead.
- Embed vs Join: Embedding avoids joins completely. Use `$lookup` when data is referenced for scalability or multi-entity sharing.

In Practice:
- Order List with Customer Details: Matching `orders.customerId` with `customers._id` produces enriched order documents displaying customer names and contact emails in admin order tables.
- Course Catalog with Instructor Bios: Courses referencing `instructorId` join with the `instructors` collection to show instructor credentials on course landing pages.

Common Pitfall: Missing an index on the `foreignField` in the joined collection, causing disastrous query slow-downs on large datasets.

What to Avoid (Unindexed $lookup Joins): Without an index on `foreignField`, MongoDB performs a full collection scan of the target collection for every document in the source collection.

Recommended Fix (Joining on Indexed Key (_id or Indexed Field)): Joining against `_id` or an indexed key allows MongoDB to use fast B-tree lookups for every join operation.

Key Takeaways:
- $lookup Stage: Joins data across collections using `from`, `localField`, `foreignField`, and `as`.
- Array Output: Matches are returned in an array field (e.g. `customer: [...]`), even for 1-to-1 matches.
- Index Requirement: Always index the `foreignField` in the target collection for acceptable join performance.

lessons.title: Atomic Updates and Transactions
lessons.subtitle: Understand single-document atomicity guarantees vs multi-document ACID transactions with sessions.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Understand single-document atomicity guarantees, multi-document ACID transactions with sessions, and consistency trade-offs.

Real-World Scenario: A money transfer subtracts money from one account and adds it to another. Both updates must succeed together. What should you consider? -> Use a transaction so both updates commit together. If one fails, abort the transaction so only one account is not changed.

Big Picture: An operation is **atomic** when it either completes as one whole operation or does not happen partly. In MongoDB, a write to a single document is atomic.

For example, increase one user's reward points:

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Single-document atomicity: MongoDB applies updates to a single document as one atomic operation without locking entire collections.
- 2. When you need a transaction: Sometimes one action must update more than one document and all updates must succeed together.
- 3. The money transfer problem: If Account A is debited but Account B fails, money vanishes unless wrapped in a transaction that can abort and roll back.
- 4. Cost and complexity: Transactions are more complex and have a cost. First consider whether the data can be designed so the operation fits inside one document. Use a multi-document transaction when the business rule truly needs several documents to change as one unit.

Core Rule (Atomicity Boundary Rule): Design schemas to capture atomic operations inside single documents where possible. Reserve multi-document ACID transactions with sessions for cross-collection invariants like financial transfers and inventory checkout.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Single-Document Atomicity: All modifications to fields and embedded arrays within a single document happen atomically without explicit transaction overhead.
- Multi-Doc Transactions: Coordinate changes across multiple documents or collections with all-or-nothing rollback semantics using client sessions.
- Document Modeling First: Careful schema design often eliminates the need for distributed transactions by embedding related state in one document.

In Practice:
- Bank Account Transfer: Debit Account A by $100 and credit Account B by $100 within a transaction session: if Account B fails or network drops, both accounts revert to their original balances.
- Order Checkout & Inventory Decrement: Creating the order document in `orders` and decrementing inventory count in `products` must either both commit or neither commit.

Common Pitfall: Executing dependent sequential updates without error handling or a transaction, leaving the database in an inconsistent corrupted state when the second operation throws.

What to Avoid (Sequential Uncoordinated Writes): If a crash or error occurs between individual writes, the database is left permanently inconsistent.

Recommended Fix (Coordinated ACID Transaction Rollback): A transaction ensures that either all operations commit, or all changes are rolled back cleanly.

Key Takeaways:
- Single-Document Atomicity: Updates to a single document are completely atomic by default in MongoDB.
- Multi-Document Transactions: Use client sessions to execute ACID transactions across multiple documents and collections.
- All-or-Nothing Rollback: If any step in a transaction fails, aborting reverts all pending mutations.

lessons.title: Database Security Basics
lessons.subtitle: Protect sensitive data using authentication, least-privilege RBAC, environment secrets, and network isolation.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Protect sensitive data with authentication, least-privilege RBAC, environment variables, and network encryption.

Real-World Scenario: A developer puts a MongoDB password directly into a public GitHub repository. What is the problem? -> Anyone who can see the code may get the password and access the database. The developer should remove the exposed secret, rotate the password, and load the new value from a secure environment variable.

Big Picture: A database can contain private information, so access must be controlled.

Remember these basic rules:
- Require authentication so users and applications must prove who they are.
- Give each database user only the permissions they need.
- Keep database passwords and connection strings out of public source code.
- Do not expose database credentials in browser code or public repositories.
- Restrict network access to trusted application servers where possible.
- Use encrypted connections when supported by the deployment.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Environment variable isolation: Credentials live in `.env` files or secret managers that are never committed to version control.
- 2. Startup validation: Check for the presence of the environment variable on server boot; fail fast if missing.
- 3. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Grant application users minimum necessary roles (e.g. `readWrite` on `learncraft` instead of `root`).
- 4. Network whitelisting: Restrict network ingress to trusted backend IPs or VPCs, never opening `0.0.0.0/0` publicly.

Core Rule (Least Privilege & Secret Isolation Rule): Never hardcode credentials or connect strings in source code. Assign dedicated database users with the least privilege necessary, require TLS encryption in transit, and isolate network access.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- No Hardcoded Secrets: Add `.env` and credential files to `.gitignore`. Use secret vaults in CI/CD and deployment environments.
- Least Privilege Roles: Create specific users with `readWrite` scoped strictly to the application database. Never run production apps as `root`.
- Network Restrictions & TLS: Bind to internal private VPC subnets and enforce TLS 1.3 encryption on connection strings (`mongodb+srv://...`).

In Practice:
- Credential Leak Remediation: If an API connection string is accidentally committed, immediately revoke and rotate the credentials on the MongoDB cluster, invalidate the Git history, and reload the secret from environment variables.
- Separate Read-Only Analytics Users: Data analysts and reporting tools should connect with a `read` role user on specific collections, preventing any chance of accidental data corruption.

Common Pitfall: Hardcoding MongoDB connection strings with plaintext passwords in client-side code or public Git repositories.

What to Avoid (Hardcoding Secrets in Source Code): Public repositories are actively crawled by automated bots that extract exposed credentials to ransom or delete databases.

Recommended Fix (Loading from Process Environment Variables): Externalizing configuration keeps sensitive secrets out of version control and allows different credentials per environment.

Key Takeaways:
- Environment Variables: Always load database URIs and secrets from external environment variables, never hardcoded strings.
- Least Privilege RBAC: Assign minimal required roles to application users rather than sharing root accounts.
- Network and TLS: Enforce encrypted connections and whitelist IP access to protected VPCs.

lessons.title: Backups, Replication, and Scaling — The Basic Idea
lessons.subtitle: Understand disaster recovery (backups), high availability (replica sets), and horizontal scaling (sharding).
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Understand the differences between disaster recovery backups, replica set high availability, and sharding for horizontal scale.

Real-World Scenario: A company wants to recover data after someone accidentally deletes records. Which idea helps? -> A backup helps recover deleted data. The company should also test the restore process so it knows the backup works.

Big Picture: These are important database ideas, but beginners do not need to configure every one of them in this lesson.

### Backups
A backup is a separate copy of data that can be used to recover after accidental deletion, corruption, or another failure. A backup is useful only if you can restore it. Teams should make backups regularly and test that recovery works.

### Replication
Replication keeps copies of data on more than one MongoDB server. It helps a deployment stay available if one server fails. A replica set is a group of MongoDB servers that maintain the same data.

### Sharding
Sharding splits data across multiple servers. It is used when one server is not enough for the size or workload of the data.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Backup: Backup helps recover data after accidental deletion, corruption, or catastrophic loss.
- 2. Replication: Replication keeps the database available (automatic failover) when a physical server crashes.
- 3. Sharding: Sharding spreads data horizontally across multiple clusters to support massive workloads and storage beyond a single machine.
- 4. Scope: These ideas are useful to recognize when reading production architecture, but detailed setup belongs in a database administration or infrastructure track.

Core Rule (Operational Boundary Rule): Maintain automated, regularly tested backups for disaster recovery. Deploy replica sets (1 Primary, 2 Secondaries) for high-availability uptime. Introduce sharding only when data volume or throughput exceeds single-node hardware capabilities.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Tested Backups: Point-in-time snapshots to restore data after human error or corruption. Backups are unverified until tested with a restore drill.
- Replica Sets: Maintains synchronized copies on multiple servers. If the Primary server fails, an automatic election promotes a Secondary in seconds.
- Sharded Clusters: Horizontal partitioning across shards driven by a shard key to distribute multi-terabyte datasets across clusters.

In Practice:
- Accidental Deletion Recovery: When an admin accidentally deletes customer records, a replica set replicates the delete to all nodes within milliseconds. The team must restore from the hourly snapshot backup to recover.
- Hardware Failure Failover: When a cloud availability zone experiences a hardware outage taking down the Primary node, the remaining replica set members elect a new Primary automatically without downtime.

Common Pitfall: Assuming a replica set replaces the need for backups, or jumping straight into sharding before optimizing queries and indexes.

What to Avoid (Assuming Replication Protects Against Deletion): Replication mirrors all write operations, including accidental deletions. Only separate backups can restore deleted data.

Recommended Fix (Automated Backups with Periodic Restore Testing): Combining replica sets for uptime with regular tested backups for recovery ensures true production resilience.

Key Takeaways:
- Backups for Recovery: Create and periodically test backups to recover from accidental deletions or corruption.
- Replication for Uptime: Replica sets maintain synchronized copies for high availability and automatic failover.
- Sharding for Scale: Sharding partitions data horizontally across clusters when workloads exceed single-node limits.

lessons.title: What Is Prisma ORM?
lessons.subtitle: Prisma ORM connects TypeScript and JavaScript applications to relational databases with type-safe models and queries.
objectives: Your Data Lives in the DB
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Understand what Prisma ORM is, why applications need a typed data-access layer, and how Prisma queries relational databases safely.

Real-World Scenario: Your application needs to show a list of users. A developer writes `prisma.user.findMany()`. What is Prisma doing here? -> Prisma sends a request to the database to get user records and returns the result to the application.

Big Picture: Prisma ORM is a tool that helps a TypeScript or JavaScript application work with a database. Instead of writing SQL for every common operation, you can use Prisma Client methods such as `findMany()` and `create()`.

Prisma does not replace the database. Your data still lives in PostgreSQL or another supported database. Prisma provides a typed way for your application to read and change that data.

Prisma Client gives TypeScript-aware queries and helps catch many mistakes while writing code. It does not remove the need to understand the database or check what a query does.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. prisma.user: Selects the User model declared in your Prisma schema.
- 2. findMany(): Asks the database for all matching records from the corresponding database table.
- 3. await: Waits asynchronously for the database request to complete.
- 4. Returned users: The returned records are stored in users with full TypeScript types.

Core Rule (The ORM Data Bridge Rule): Prisma ORM acts as a type-safe bridge between application code and the database. It generates TypeScript types directly from your database schema, preventing runtime type mismatches.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- End-to-End Type Safety: Prisma Client queries return strongly typed TypeScript objects matching your exact schema fields, catching typos at compile time.
- Database Stays In Control: Prisma does not replace PostgreSQL or SQLite. Your database manages storage, constraints, indexes, and transactions while Prisma streamlines querying.
- Intuitive Client Methods: Methods like findMany, create, update, and delete express database actions cleanly without hand-written SQL queries.

In Practice:
- Prisma Client vs Raw SQL Concatenation: Raw string SQL queries lack autocomplete, risk syntax typos, and easily lead to SQL injection if variables are concatenated manually. Prisma Client methods provide autocomplete and parameterize queries automatically.
- Model Centric Design: Every table in your database maps to a Prisma model. Changes in the schema immediately reflect in TypeScript types when running prisma generate.

Common Pitfall: Assuming Prisma replaces the database or that database constraints are no longer necessary.

What to Avoid (Relying Solely on App-Level Validation): Without database-level constraints like @unique, concurrent requests can insert duplicate records even if app-level validation checks first.

Recommended Fix (Enforcing Constraints in Prisma Schema): The database enforces unique email integrity at the storage level, guaranteeing zero duplicates even under heavy concurrency.

Why It Matters: An ORM makes querying easier, but the database remains the ultimate authority on data integrity, constraints, and durability.

Key Takeaways:
- Prisma is an ORM: Prisma provides a typed way to read and modify data in relational databases like PostgreSQL.
- Your Data Lives in the DB: Prisma does not replace your database; it issues optimized queries against your underlying database engine.
- TypeScript Integration: Prisma Client queries are generated from your schema, giving autocomplete and compile-time error checking.

const users = await prisma.user.findMany();

console.log(users);

lessons.title: Prisma Project Setup and Main Files
lessons.subtitle: Understand the key files in a Prisma project: schema.prisma, configuration, Prisma Client, and migrations.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Explore the main files of a Prisma project: schema.prisma, configuration files, generated Prisma Client, and migrations directory.

Real-World Scenario: You open a project and cannot find the database URL inside `schema.prisma`. Does this mean the project cannot connect to the database? -> No. In Prisma 7, the URL is normally placed in `prisma.config.ts`. In Prisma 5/6, it is in `schema.prisma`. Check the project's configuration file or environment variables.

Big Picture: A Prisma project has a few important files. Their exact locations can vary by project, but their jobs are similar:

- The Prisma schema (`prisma/schema.prisma`) describes models and their fields.
- `prisma.config.ts` holds Prisma CLI configuration, including the database URL in Prisma 7 (or directly in `schema.prisma` with `url = env("DATABASE_URL")` in Prisma 5 and 6).
- Prisma Client is generated from the schema and used by application code.
- The migrations folder (`prisma/migrations/`) stores the history of database structure changes.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. generator client: Configures the client generator and where the generated client code is written.
- 2. datasource db: Sets the database provider (e.g. postgresql, mysql, sqlite).
- 3. prisma.config.ts: Defines CLI configuration and provides the database URL in Prisma 7 projects.
- 4. Version compatibility: In Prisma 5/6 (used in this project), the URL is declared directly inside datasource in schema.prisma: url = env("DATABASE_URL").

Core Rule (Single Source of Truth Rule): The Prisma schema is the declarative single source of truth for your data models. Configuration files tell the CLI how to connect and where to generate the client.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- schema.prisma: Defines models, fields, relations, enums, and generator settings for your database.
- Connection & Config: Stores database URLs via env variables, keeping sensitive credentials out of version control.
- migrations/ Directory: Contains chronological SQL migration files representing the full evolution of your database schema.

In Practice:
- Prisma 5/6 vs Prisma 7 Configuration: In Prisma 5/6 (such as LearnCraft's current setup), datasource contains url = env("DATABASE_URL"). In Prisma 7, CLI configuration and connection URLs are moved to prisma.config.ts for cleaner separation of schema definition and environment config.
- Environment Variable Safety: Always keep database credentials in a .env file and never commit secrets to version control. Reference credentials using env("DATABASE_URL").

Common Pitfall: Hardcoding database connection URLs in schema files or committing production credentials.

What to Avoid (Hardcoding Database Credentials): Exposes database passwords in git history and prevents environment-specific database switching (dev vs staging vs prod).

Recommended Fix (Using Environment Variables): Keeps credentials secure in .env and allows different connection URLs for local development and cloud production.

Why It Matters: Securing database connection strings is critical for preventing unauthorized database access and data breaches.

Key Takeaways:
- Schema as Foundation: schema.prisma defines the structure of your data and models.
- Secure Environment URLs: Always load database connection strings from environment variables via env("DATABASE_URL").
- Migrations History: The prisma/migrations folder tracks database schema changes over time.

lessons.title: Prisma Schema and Models
lessons.subtitle: Define application entities, tables, and fields using declarative Prisma models.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Define application entities, tables, fields, and constraints using declarative Prisma schema models.

Real-World Scenario: You are building a course app. You need to store each course's title and description in the database. Where should you describe this in Prisma? -> In a `Course` model in the Prisma schema. The model describes which fields each course has.

Big Picture: A model represents an entity in your application, such as a user, a course, or a blog post. In a relational database, a model usually maps to a table.

Inside a model, you describe the fields that every record of that kind will have.

Each field has a name and a type. Attributes such as `@id` and `@unique` give extra meaning to a field.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. model User: Defines a User model, which maps to a table in the database.
- 2. id Int @id: id is the primary key and autoincrement() generates the next number automatically.
- 3. email String @unique: email is text, and @unique makes sure no two users have the same email.
- 4. name String: name is a required text field.
- 5. createdAt DateTime @default(now()): createdAt saves the date and time when the record is created.

Core Rule (Model-to-Table Mapping Rule): Every model in schema.prisma maps to a physical database table, and every field maps to a column with a matching SQL type and constraint.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- @id Attribute: Every model must have a primary key field identified by @id so individual records can be uniquely located.
- @default Function: Generates automatic initial values like autoincrement() for IDs or now() for timestamps.
- @unique Constraint: Prevents duplicate values across records, creating a unique database index.

In Practice:
- Designing a Course Model: A Course entity needs an identifier, a title, a slug for SEO-friendly URLs, and publishing status.
- Naming Conventions: Prisma convention uses PascalCase for model names (User, Course, Post) and camelCase for field names (createdAt, authorId).

Common Pitfall: Omitting a primary key `@id` from a model definition.

What to Avoid (Model Without a Primary Key): Prisma will fail to validate the schema with an error stating that the model must define a primary key.

Recommended Fix (Defining an Explicit Primary Key): Provides a unique identifier for finding, updating, and deleting individual articles.

Why It Matters: Relational databases require a primary key to uniquely distinguish and index rows.

Key Takeaways:
- Models Represent Tables: Each model represents an entity table with named, typed fields.
- Every Model Needs @id: An @id primary key attribute is required to identify records.
- Attributes Add Constraints: Attributes like @unique and @default add business rules directly to the database.

Designing a Course Model
codeBlocks.code:
model Course {
  id          Int      @id @default(autoincrement())
  slug        String   @unique
  title       String
  description String?
  isPublished Boolean  @default(false)
  createdAt   DateTime @default(now())
}

lessons.title: Field Types and Schema Attributes
lessons.subtitle: Use scalar types, optional fields, defaults, and attributes to model precise database columns.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Use scalar types (String, Int, Decimal, DateTime), optional nullable fields, and default value attributes.

Real-World Scenario: A product may not have details when it is first added. How can the Prisma schema allow a missing description without failing? -> Make the field optional with `String?`. Then the value can be text or `null`.

Big Picture: Prisma supports common field types such as `String`, `Int`, `Boolean`, `DateTime`, and `Decimal`. You can make a field optional by adding `?` after its type.

Attributes such as `@default()` provide initial values when a record is created. Optional fields allow `null` values for missing information.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. String vs String?: String requires text; String? allows optional text or null.
- 2. price Decimal: Decimal is ideal for money because it avoids rounding issues common to floating-point numbers.
- 3. inStock Boolean @default(true): Boolean stores true or false; @default(true) sets inStock to true if no value is provided.
- 4. createdAt DateTime @default(now()): DateTime stores timestamps; @default(now()) sets the creation time automatically.

Core Rule (Exact Types & Optionality Rule): Fields without '?' are NOT NULL in SQL and required in TypeScript. Fields with '?' are nullable in SQL and allow undefined or null in TypeScript.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Nullable with '?': Adding '?' makes a field nullable in the database and optional in TypeScript input objects.
- Decimal for Money: Float can suffer from IEEE-754 precision rounding errors. Always use Decimal for currency and prices.
- Sensible Defaults: @default(true) or @default(false) ensures fields always have a valid state without requiring manual assignment.

In Practice:
- Why Decimal Beats Float for Currency: In JavaScript and SQL, Float (0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004) can cause fractional cent discrepancies. Prisma Decimal maps to exact PostgreSQL NUMERIC.
- Timestamp Tracking with @updatedAt: Prisma provides @updatedAt, an attribute that automatically updates a DateTime field whenever a record is modified.

Common Pitfall: Using Float instead of Decimal for financial amounts.

What to Avoid (Using Float for Prices): Summing Float amounts can result in values like 19.990000000000002, failing exact financial audits.

Recommended Fix (Using Decimal for Money): Guarantees exact two-decimal precision for accounting and payments.

Why It Matters: Financial applications require exact mathematical precision that Float cannot guarantee.

Key Takeaways:
- Optional Fields Use '?': String? allows null values, while String requires a value.
- Decimal for Financial Data: Use Decimal rather than Float to avoid rounding inaccuracies in pricing.
- Default Values: Attributes like @default(true) and @default(now()) populate missing values automatically.

codeBlocks.code:
model Product {
  id          Int      @id @default(autoincrement())
  title       String
  description String?
  price       Decimal
  inStock     Boolean  @default(true)
  createdAt   DateTime @default(now())
}

lessons.title: What Is Prisma Client?
lessons.subtitle: Prisma Client is the generated type-safe query engine your application uses to read and write database records.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Learn how Prisma Client is generated from the schema and provides typed methods for reading and changing data.

Real-World Scenario: You add a new `phone` field to the `User` model, but TypeScript does not recognize `phone` in Prisma queries. What should you check? -> Check that the schema was updated and Prisma Client was generated again. Also check that the application imports the correct generated client.

Big Picture: Prisma Client is the generated code your application uses to query the database. Prisma creates it from your models, so the available models and fields are reflected in TypeScript types and editor suggestions.

In Prisma 7, direct connections use a database driver adapter such as `@prisma/adapter-pg`. In Prisma 5 and 6 (as used in this project), PrismaClient is imported directly from `@prisma/client` and connects using `DATABASE_URL`.

Prisma Client is the part of Prisma you use most often in application code. It provides typed methods for reading and changing data.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Import PrismaClient: Imports the client generated specifically for your application models.
- 2. Driver adapter / connection: Prisma 7 uses driver adapters like PrismaPg; Prisma 5/6 initializes directly with built-in connection handling.
- 3. Pass connection parameters: The database connection string is passed securely via process.env.DATABASE_URL.
- 4. Export singleton instance: Exports a single shared client instance so the application reuses connections instead of creating new sockets per request.

Core Rule (Regeneration Rule): Whenever schema.prisma changes, you must run 'prisma generate' to recompile Prisma Client types. Without regeneration, TypeScript and runtime queries remain outdated.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- npx prisma generate: Reads schema.prisma and emits custom TypeScript definitions tailored specifically to your models.
- Full IDE Autocomplete: Field names, relational filters, and selection arguments are suggested and validated directly by your code editor.
- Singleton Client: Instantiate one PrismaClient instance per application process to maintain connection pool efficiency.

In Practice:
- Schema Change Workflow: 1. Edit schema.prisma (e.g. add a new column). 2. Run 'npx prisma migrate dev' or 'npx prisma generate'. 3. Immediately access the new field on prisma.model in TypeScript.
- Generated Type Exports: Prisma also exports type definitions such as 'User' and 'Prisma.UserCreateInput' directly from the client package for use in function signatures and API request types.

Common Pitfall: Forgetting to run `prisma generate` after editing `schema.prisma`.

What to Avoid (Editing Schema Without Generating): TypeScript throws compilation errors because the generated client node_modules files still reflect the old schema.

Recommended Fix (Running Prisma Generate): Prisma Client is synchronized with the schema and TypeScript types validate without error.

Why It Matters: Client generation synchronizes your code editor, TypeScript compiler, and runtime query methods with your actual schema.

Key Takeaways:
- Generated Query Engine: Prisma Client is custom-generated TypeScript code built directly from your schema.
- Instant Autocomplete: Queries benefit from compile-time type validation and editor suggestions.
- Regenerate on Schema Changes: Always run 'prisma generate' after modifying schema.prisma.

lessons.title: Create and Read Records
lessons.subtitle: Insert new records with create() and retrieve records with findMany(), findUnique(), and findFirst().
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Insert rows with create() and read data with findMany(), findUnique(), and findFirst().

Real-World Scenario: A user opens a profile page using their email address. Which method is suitable to find that user? -> Use `findUnique()` with the email field, because the email identifies at most one user.

Big Picture: Prisma Client has dedicated methods for adding records and reading records.

- `create()` inserts a new record with provided data.
- `findMany()` fetches multiple records matching optional criteria.
- `findUnique()` finds exactly one record by a unique field or primary key.
- `findFirst()` finds the first record that matches a general condition.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. create({ data }): Takes a data object containing required fields and inserts a new row in the database.
- 2. findMany(): Fetches a list of records. Without arguments, it returns all records in the table.
- 3. findUnique({ where }): where must specify a field marked with @id or @unique in the schema, guaranteeing at most one row is returned.
- 4. Null return on missing: If no matching record exists, findUnique returns null rather than throwing an exception.

Core Rule (Unique Lookup Rule): findUnique() can only query fields marked with @id, @unique, or composite unique constraints (@@unique). For arbitrary non-unique fields, use findFirst() or findMany().

Why It Matters & Rules:
- create(): Inserts a single row and returns the freshly created object including generated IDs and timestamps.
- findMany(): Returns an array of records. Accepts filtering, sorting, pagination, and relation includes.
- findUnique(): Optimized single-row query by primary key or unique index. Returns the record or null if not found.

In Practice:
- findUnique vs findFirst: Use findUnique when searching by ID, UUID, or unique email. Use findFirst when filtering by non-unique fields like role or status.
- createMany for Bulk Inserts: To insert many records in a single database roundtrip, Prisma provides createMany({ data: [...] }), significantly faster than looping create().

Common Pitfall: Using `findUnique()` with a non-unique field.

What to Avoid (findUnique with Non-Unique Field): TypeScript will reject this query because findUnique only accepts fields with unique database indexes.

Recommended Fix (Using findFirst or findMany): TypeScript compiles cleanly and the query fetches the first matching record.

Why It Matters: Enforcing unique constraints at the type level prevents bugs caused by expecting one result when multiple exist.

Key Takeaways:
- create() Inserts Rows: Pass a data object with required fields to insert a record.
- findUnique() for Primary Keys: Use findUnique with unique fields to fetch a single record or null.
- findMany() for Collections: Fetches an array of records matching your criteria.

lessons.title: Update and Delete Records
lessons.subtitle: Modify existing rows with update() and remove records safely with delete() and deleteMany().
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Modify existing records with update() and remove rows safely with delete() and deleteMany().

Real-World Scenario: A user edits their profile name. Should you create a new user or update the existing user? -> Update the existing user with `update()`, using the user's unique ID to find the record and passing the new name in `data`.

Big Picture: Prisma Client provides `update()` and `delete()` to modify or remove existing records.

- `update()` targets a single record using a unique identifier and applies changes in `data`.
- `delete()` removes a single record matching a unique identifier.
- For bulk modifications, Prisma provides `updateMany()` and `deleteMany()`.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. update({ where, data }): Locates the record using a unique identifier in where, and applies new values provided in data.
- 2. Atomic partial updates: You only need to supply the fields being changed in data; unmentioned fields remain untouched.
- 3. delete({ where }): Permanently removes the specified record from the database.
- 4. Return values: Both update() and delete() return the affected record.

Core Rule (Unique Target Rule for update/delete): Single-record update() and delete() methods require a unique 'where' selector. If the targeted record does not exist, Prisma throws a RecordNotFound error (P2025).

Why It Matters & Rules:
- update(): Updates specified fields of a single record identified by unique key. Returns the modified record.
- delete(): Deletes a specific record by primary key or unique index. Throws P2025 if the record does not exist.
- updateMany / deleteMany: Applies mutations or deletions across multiple rows matching a where filter. Returns a count object.

In Practice:
- Atomic Number Increments: Prisma supports atomic number updates like increment and decrement to avoid race conditions when counters change concurrently.
- Soft Deletes vs Hard Deletes: Instead of permanently removing rows with delete(), many production systems implement soft deletes by updating a deletedAt timestamp (e.g. data: { deletedAt: new Date() }).

Common Pitfall: Calling `update()` on an ID that might not exist, causing unhandled P2025 exceptions.

What to Avoid (Unchecked update() Call): Prisma throws PrismaClientKnownRequestError with code P2025, which crashes the route handler if uncaught.

Recommended Fix (Handling Missing Records or Using upsert()): Gracefully handles nonexistent records without unexpected application crashes.

Why It Matters: Production web applications must handle missing entity mutations predictably without crashing API servers.

Key Takeaways:
- update() Modifies Existing Data: Target by unique ID and provide only the fields being changed in data.
- delete() Removes Records: Deletes a single record by unique identifier and returns the deleted row.
- upsert() for Idempotency: Use upsert() when you want to update an existing record or create it if missing.

lessons.title: Filtering and Sorting Data
lessons.subtitle: Filter query results with where conditions and order results with orderBy.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Filter results using where conditions and sort records with orderBy in ascending or descending order.

Real-World Scenario: A blog needs to show only published posts, with the newest post at the top. What Prisma query should you write? -> Use `where: { published: true }` to filter the posts and `orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" }` to sort by newest first.

Big Picture: You can filter which records to return using `where` and sort their order using `orderBy`.

- `where` filters rows by comparing fields against values or operators (e.g. `equals`, `contains`, `gt`, `lt`, `in`).
- `orderBy` sorts rows ascending (`"asc"`) or descending (`"desc"`).

Prisma turns these into SQL `WHERE` and `ORDER BY` clauses.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. where: { published: true }: Filters rows so only records where published is true are retrieved from the database.
- 2. orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" }: Sorts matching posts descending by creation date, placing the newest posts first.
- 3. Combined in one query: Both filtering and sorting happen inside the database engine before rows are transmitted over the network.

Core Rule (Database-Level Filtering Rule): Always filter with where and sort with orderBy in the database query. Filtering in application memory wastes network bandwidth and database memory.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- where Clause: Filters rows using equality, ranges (gt, gte, lt, lte), pattern matches (contains), or sets (in).
- orderBy Clause: Sorts records by one or multiple fields in 'asc' (ascending) or 'desc' (descending) order.
- AND / OR Operators: Combine multiple conditions using AND, OR, and NOT logical filter arrays.

In Practice:
- Range & Text Filtering: Prisma provides operators for price ranges, string searches, and status lists.
- Sorting by Multiple Fields: You can pass an array to orderBy to sort by multiple columns, such as sorting first by category ascending and then by price descending.

Common Pitfall: Fetching all records and filtering with JavaScript array methods in memory.

What to Avoid (Filtering in Memory with Array.filter): Transfers thousands of unnecessary rows across the database connection, causing high memory usage and slow responses.

Recommended Fix (Filtering in the Database Query): Database uses indexes to find matching rows instantly and transmits only the needed data.

Why It Matters: Pushing filtering and sorting to the database engine ensures high performance as your dataset grows.

Key Takeaways:
- where Filters Rows: Specify conditions in where to filter records in the database.
- orderBy Sorts Results: Use 'asc' for oldest/lowest and 'desc' for newest/highest.
- Filter in DB, Not App: Always filter inside the database query rather than in JavaScript memory.

lessons.title: Select Only the Fields You Need
lessons.subtitle: Use select to retrieve only necessary columns, improving performance and protecting sensitive data.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Use select to retrieve only the required fields, protecting sensitive data and reducing payload sizes.

Real-World Scenario: Your user table has an internal password hash, but a page only needs the user's name and email. How does `select` help? -> Use `select` to return only `name` and `email`. Do not fetch or send the password hash to the client.

Big Picture: By default, Prisma Client returns all scalar fields of a model. If a model has 20 columns, a query loads all 20.

Using `select`, you specify only the fields your application needs for that screen or operation. This reduces memory usage, speeds up database transfers, and prevents sensitive fields (like password hashes or API tokens) from leaking.

In TypeScript, the returned object type automatically adjusts to contain only the selected fields.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. select object: Pass an object mapping desired field names to true.
- 2. Excluded fields: Any field not specified (such as passwordHash or internalNotes) is omitted from the SQL SELECT query.
- 3. TypeScript narrowing: TypeScript types are narrowed automatically so attempting to access omitted fields results in a compiler error.
- 4. select vs include: select chooses which fields of the current model to load; include eagerly loads entire relation models.

Core Rule (Least Privilege Data Rule): Never query or transmit fields that the receiving UI or API client does not require. Always use select to exclude password hashes, secret tokens, and heavy binary payloads.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Prevent Data Leaks: Prevents sensitive attributes like passwordHash, resetTokens, or SSNs from being fetched into memory or sent in API responses.
- Slim Payload Size: Minimizes serialization time, database network transfer, and memory consumption by skipping heavy text and JSON fields.
- Compiler Guaranteed: TypeScript ensures your UI code cannot mistakenly read fields that were not fetched in the select clause.

In Practice:
- Excluding Passwords Safely: Instead of manually deleting passwordHash from user objects after fetching, use select so the database never reads the hash in the first place.
- Mutual Exclusivity of select and include: In Prisma, select and include cannot be used as top-level siblings on the same model. To fetch a relation alongside selected fields, put a nested select or include inside select.

Common Pitfall: Using `select` and `include` together at the same level.

What to Avoid (Mixing select and include as Siblings): Prisma throws a validation error because select and include cannot be combined at the same query level.

Recommended Fix (Nesting the Relation Inside select): Selects specific fields of the parent model while cleanly fetching the related posts.

Why It Matters: Understanding Prisma's selection syntax prevents frustrating query structure errors.

Key Takeaways:
- select Limits Columns: Specify only the fields you need instead of fetching all table columns.
- Protects Sensitive Fields: Omit password hashes and internal tokens directly at the database query level.
- Type Narrowing: TypeScript guarantees that only selected fields exist on the result object.

lessons.title: Understand Relationships Between Models
lessons.subtitle: Master connections between models: relation fields, foreign keys, 1-to-1, 1-to-N, and M-to-N.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Connect models using relation scalar fields (foreign keys) and virtual relation fields with @relation.

Real-World Scenario: A user can write many blog posts, but each post belongs to one author. Which relationship is this, and where is the foreign key stored? -> It is a one-to-many relationship from User to Post. One user can have many posts, and each post stores the `authorId` foreign key referencing the user.

Big Picture: Real applications connect models together. For example, a user writes posts, an order contains items, or a student enrolls in courses.

Prisma uses two parts to create a relationship:

- A relation scalar field (`authorId Int`) that stores the foreign key column in the database table.
- A relation field (`author User @relation(...)`) that Prisma uses in TypeScript to represent the connected model.

The relation field does not exist as a physical column in the SQL database; Prisma uses it to generate queries and typed joins.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. posts Post[]: A virtual relation field on User indicating one user can have multiple related Post records.
- 2. authorId Int: The relation scalar field that physically stores the foreign key in the database table.
- 3. @relation(fields, references): Tells Prisma that authorId in Post links to id in User.
- 4. Database integrity: Prisma creates a foreign key constraint in the database, preventing orphaned posts with invalid authorIds.

Core Rule (Virtual Field vs Physical Foreign Key Rule): Foreign key scalar fields (like authorId) physically exist in the database table. Relation fields (like author or posts) are virtual helpers Prisma uses to navigate relations in application code.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Relation Scalar Field: The concrete database column (e.g. authorId) storing the reference ID. It exists as a real SQL column.
- Relation Field: A typed field (e.g. author User or posts Post[]) used by Prisma Client to load and traverse relations.
- Referential Integrity: Database foreign keys ensure related parent records exist and enforce deletion rules like CASCADE or RESTRICT.

In Practice:
- One-to-One (1:1) and Many-to-Many (M:N): In a 1:1 relation (User to Profile), the foreign key column is marked @unique. In Many-to-Many (Post to Tag), Prisma supports implicit relations with an automatic join table.
- Referential Actions on Delete: You can specify onDelete: Cascade on the relation attribute to automatically delete child posts when a parent user is deleted.

Common Pitfall: Declaring a relation field without providing the corresponding foreign key scalar field in `@relation`.

What to Avoid (Missing Foreign Key Scalar Field): Prisma schema validation fails because fields in @relation must name an actual scalar field in the model.

Recommended Fix (Declaring Both Scalar and Relation Fields): Prisma validates cleanly, creates the foreign key constraint, and provides typed relations.

Why It Matters: Relational integrity requires a physical column to store the reference ID.

Key Takeaways:
- Relation Scalar vs Relation Field: authorId stores the foreign key column; author is the virtual navigation field.
- @relation Connects Models: The @relation attribute maps foreign key fields to primary keys.
- Automatic Foreign Key Constraints: Prisma creates database constraints to ensure related parent records exist.

lessons.title: Read Related Records with `include` and Nested `select`
lessons.subtitle: Eagerly load related entities using include or fetch precise nested subsets using nested select.
objectives: Relations Are Not Loaded by Default
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Eagerly load related models with include or fetch specific nested subsets with nested select.

Real-World Scenario: A profile page needs the user's name and the titles of their posts, but not the full post contents. Should you use `include` or nested `select`? -> Use `select` for the user's name and a nested `select` for each post's title.

Big Picture: By default, querying a user does not fetch their posts. This keeps queries fast and avoids pulling extra data from the database.

When you need related records, you have two choices:

- `include`: Loads the user and all fields of the related posts.
- Nested `select`: Chooses exactly which fields to return from the user and which fields to return from each related post.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. include: { posts: true }: Tells Prisma to fetch all scalar fields of the User plus all scalar fields of every related Post in one operation.
- 2. Nested select: Selects specific columns on both the parent model and related child models.
- 3. Avoids N+1 query problem: Prisma batches relation queries efficiently, preventing slow loops of individual queries.
- 4. Strongly typed results: The returned TypeScript shape includes the related array with exact field typing.

Core Rule (Include vs Select Choice Rule): Use include when you need all scalar fields of the parent plus all fields of related children. Use nested select when you only need a specific subset of columns to keep payloads lean.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- include: Loads the entire related entity alongside the parent model. Simple and fast for full details views.
- Nested select: Specifies exact fields across parent and child relations, reducing memory and bandwidth.
- N+1 Prevention: Prisma optimizes relation queries using SQL JOINs or batched IN queries, avoiding sequential latency.

In Practice:
- Filtering Nested Relations: You can apply where, orderBy, and take inside include or select to filter which related items are returned.
- TypeScript Return Types: Prisma provides helper types like Prisma.UserGetPayload<{ include: { posts: true } }> when passing relations to utility functions.

Common Pitfall: Accidentally fetching huge relational trees (e.g. users -> all posts -> all comments -> all authors).

What to Avoid (Over-Fetching Deep Relational Trees): Can fetch tens of thousands of rows and megabytes of JSON, slowing database queries and freezing servers.

Recommended Fix (Using Selective Projection and Limits): Keeps database response times under a few milliseconds and payload sizes minimal.

Why It Matters: Controlling relation depth and payload size is essential for production performance and scalability.

Key Takeaways:
- Relations Are Not Loaded by Default: Prisma queries do not fetch relations unless explicitly instructed.
- include for Full Models: Use include to eager-load all fields of related entities.
- Nested select for Slim Payloads: Pick specific columns on related records to optimize performance.

lessons.title: Create Related Records with Nested Writes
lessons.subtitle: Create, link, and manage parent and child records in a single atomic database operation.
lessons.summaryText:
Overview: Create and connect parent and child records in a single atomic database operation using nested writes.

Real-World Scenario: When a customer signs up, your application also needs to create their first profile record. Why is a nested write helpful? -> Use a nested write. Create the customer and the related profile in one Prisma operation so both records are saved together.

Big Picture: A nested write lets you create a record and its related records in a single operation. Instead of creating a user first, waiting for the generated ID, and then creating posts with that ID, Prisma does both together.

Prisma handles creating the parent, capturing its generated foreign key, and inserting the related children inside a single database transaction.

Prisma nested writes also support connecting existing records using `connect` or `connectOrCreate`.

Key Breakdown:
- 1. Parent create: Creates the new User record and generates its primary key.
- 2. posts: { create: [...] }: Creates the related Post records and automatically assigns their authorId foreign key to the new user's ID.
- 3. Atomic transaction: Prisma wraps the parent and child inserts in an atomic database transaction. If creating a post fails, the user is rolled back.
- 4. Single roundtrip: Eliminates manual foreign key plumbing in application code.

Core Rule (Atomic Nested Write Rule): Prisma executes nested writes inside a database transaction automatically. If any child creation fails, all changes roll back, preventing orphan records.

Why It Matters & Rules:
- Automatic Transaction: Both parent and child inserts succeed together or fail together with zero partial writes.
- connect & connectOrCreate: Link to existing records by unique ID or create them if they do not exist yet.
- Zero Manual Plumbing: No need to capture user.id and pass authorId: user.id manually across sequential queries.

In Practice:
- Connecting Existing Records with connect: When creating a post, you can link it to an existing author using connect instead of passing the raw authorId.
- connectOrCreate for Idempotent Setup: Useful for tags and categories: connects to an existing tag with that name or creates the tag if it is missing.

Common Pitfall: Creating parent and child records in separate manual steps without transaction protection.

What to Avoid (Sequential Manual Inserts Without a Transaction): If the second query fails due to network drop or validation, the database is left with incomplete orphaned data.

Recommended Fix (Using a Single Nested Write): Prisma executes both inserts in a transaction; failure rolls back everything cleanly.

Why It Matters: Data integrity depends on related entities either existing completely or not at all.

Key Takeaways:
- Atomic Creation: Parent and child records are created together in a single transaction.
- Automatic ID Wiring: Prisma sets the child's foreign key automatically to the parent's generated ID.
- connect & connectOrCreate: Use connect to link existing records and connectOrCreate for safe setup.
